articles.title: Malaria Parasite Caught in the Act of Breaking and Entering
articles.summary: To invade red blood cells, the deadly protist creates a temporary molecular portal that disappears behind it — a door we can now see in fine detail. The post Malaria Parasite Caught in the Act of Breaking and Entering first appeared on Quanta Magazine

Comments Read Later Read Later biophysics Malaria Parasite Caught in the Act of Breaking and Entering By Joanna Thompson October 23, 2026 To invade red blood cells, the deadly protists create temporary molecular portals that disappear behind them — doors we can now see in fine detail. Read Later Add as Preferred Source (opens in a new tab) i Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results. Plasmodium , the parasite that causes malaria, invades and proliferates inside red blood cells. Researchers imaged the proteins (dark purple ovals) it places on the cell membrane that let it slip through unnoticed. Ada Zejun Shen for Quanta Magazine Introduction In medieval Italy, it was accepted wisdom that anyone walking near a swamp risked falling ill from “bad air” — mala aria . Victims were struck with fever, headache, nausea, and chills, and occasionally the illness escalated to vomiting, jaundice, and death. Today, we still call this affliction malaria. For much of human history, it has ravaged populations in humid tropical and subtropical regions, killing untold numbers. In the 20th century, it was responsible for up to 5% of deaths worldwide; it still kills approximately 600,000 people each year. What malaria was and how it infected humans was deeply mysterious until barely 150 years ago. In 1880, the French physician Charles Louis Alphonse Laveran peered at a sample of a soldier’s blood through a crude microscope and discovered the true cause of the disease: not miasma, but a genus of shape-shifting single-celled protists called Plasmodium . Since then, scientists and doctors have described in precise detail the parasites’ life cycle, hosts, and disease progression, and even the nuances of various Plasmodium species, which present slightly different forms of the disease. But some crucial aspects have remained a mystery. For example, Plasmodium invades human red blood cells as part of its life cycle. To get in, the microbe creates a ring-shaped structure called the moving junction, which briefly creates a gap in the cell membrane it can slip through. The gap then disappears without a trace. It opens and closes so rapidly, at such a small scale, that imaging technologies couldn’t capture it. Researchers had no clue what the portal structure actually looked like. “Because of that,” said Chi-Min Ho , a microbiologist and structural biologist at Columbia University, “we didn’t really know anything about how it works.” Now, Ho’s lab has imaged the moving junction right at the moment of invasion, in unprecedented detail. Her team found that when the Plasmodium parasite installs molecular gaskets in the host cell, it radically remodels the cell membrane to slip through without a trace. This knowledge could help inform the next generation of malaria treatments and influence the drug-discovery process for other parasitic diseases, such as cyclosporiasis and toxoplasmosis. “It’s a totally mind-blowing paper,” said Jake Baum , a parasitologist at the University of New South Wales, who was not involved in the research. “At the end of the day, this is not molecular biology. This is biophysics.” Home Remodeling The history of malaria research has paralleled advances in microscopy, from the development of simple light microscopes like the one Laveran used to the cutting-edge cryo-electron techniques of Ho’s lab. This is because the cells the microbes invade are extremely tiny — and the parasites are even smaller. At about 8 micrometers across, red blood cells are among the smallest cells in the human body, and all species of Plasmodium are a fraction of that size during the invasion stage. Attempts to image the parasites in the act of breaking and entering got off the ground in the 1970s, when pioneering microbiologists first applied electron microscopy. These scientists observed a distinct thickening of the cellular membrane near the parasite’s access point. Then the tiny, round Plasmodium seemed to simply merge with the cell, like a water droplet coalescing into a larger pool. It would be decades before techniques developed enough to isolate the proteins that make this possible, much less image them. James Dvorak’s lab at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases took the first microscopic videos of Plasmodium parasites entering a red blood cell. This one was filmed in 1978. Arrows point to parasite entry points. Courtesy of Jake Baum Another hurdle is that malaria parasites have a very complicated life cycle . They are most at home in the gut of a mosquito where they can reproduce sexually. Humans are what’s known as a reservoir host — a place for the parasite to live while it waits to be taken up by an insect. “The food supply happens to be our red blood cells,” said Kirk Deitsch , a microbiologist and immunologist at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York. “That’s why they’re invading us.” To this end, the Plasmodium parasite assumes a variety of shapes and sizes as it moves through its life stages: Sometimes it’s shaped like an egg, sometimes a spindly thread, sometimes a gangly starfish. It can move through this cycle in rapid succession or hang out in one stage (the hypnozoite phase in the human liver) for years. When it enters its tiny, round merozoite stage, the parasite is ready to invade a red blood cell. Plasmodium pulls up to the scene of the crime with all the proteins and other biological equipment it needs. The entry procedure is more delicate than simply punching a hole in the host cell. “If you’re trying to push an orange into a balloon, the balloon mustn’t pop, right?” Baum said. Based on previous research, scientists knew the broad strokes of this process. The parasite approaches a host red blood cell and inserts a ring of protein anchors into the cell’s membrane. Collectively these anchors are known as the moving junction. Plasmodium locks into them with proteins expressed on its surface — and then pushes forward. The moving junction forms a continuous portal in the host cell membrane for the parasite to travel through. Once the parasite is fully inside, the cell membrane seals up behind it. The whole process takes less than a minute. Ho and the other authors of the new paper used cryo-electron microscopy to probe the four individual protein units in each anchor. What they learned allowed them to propose a more detailed model for how the moving junction actively remodels the host cell’s membrane. The parasite injects into the red blood cell three proteins, which form a dense wedge beneath the membrane surface; a fourth protein connects this structure to the invader. Plasmodium places many of these anchors on the red blood cell surface. The proteins produce electrostatic forces and pressure in the cell membrane, which crowd and displace its lipid molecules. This deforms the membrane and reverses its curvature. It bows slightly inward around the parasite — in fact, some lipids slough off and reassemble into a protective membrane for the invader — before re-forming and sealing behind it. “It’s a really nice example of how a field has built step by step by step toward a really powerful observation,” Baum said. A visualization of four proteins in the moving junction anchor complex. The electrostatic properties of these proteins destabilize the membrane’s lipid bilayer and deform it, letting the parasite slip through. Courtesy of Chi-Min Ho Once inside, Plasmodium approaches its remodeling work more comprehensively. Red blood cells are essentially bags of hemoglobin; they have no nucleus or organelles to speak of. So Plasmodium builds from the ground up. It secretes proteins that allow it to feed on hemoglobin, remove waste, and stretch the cell’s cytoplasm. Ho compared it to the conversion of an empty warehouse floor into a stylish lofted apartment. “It’s putting in plumbing,” she said. “It’s putting in the floors. It’s literally building everything for itself.” In this process, the parasite also redecorates the cell’s exterior. It is equipped with genes that allow it to make a series of distinct but closely related adhesive proteins that it can express on the red blood cell’s surface. These proteins cause the cells to stick to the walls of the blood vessels around them — one of the main causes of malaria’s painful symptoms. In 2025, research from Deitsch’s lab found that by periodically switching between proteins, the parasite can avoid tipping off the immune system to its presence for days or weeks at a time. Such extensive exterior cellular remodeling serves a purpose: It helps Plasmodium avoid a trip to the spleen, an organ that filters out dead, defective, or broken red blood cells as well as any undercover parasites. Protrusions called knobs cover the surface of an infected red blood cell. Plasmodium , the parasite that causes malaria, expresses these proteins after it invades the cell. They make cells clump to the walls of blood vessels, causing the disease’s most dangerous symptoms including organ distress, seizures, and coma. Rick Fairhurst and Jordan Zuspann, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National Institutes of Health The parasite itself undergoes a radical change inside the cell. It transforms from a roundish merozoite into an amoebalike trophozoite. It grows several cytoplasm “arms” and flattens out, said Christiaan van Ooij , a molecular parasitologist at Keele University in the United Kingdom. This also helps it evade the immune system. The trophozoite shape is more flexible than that of the spherical merozoite, and the immune system clocks supple cells as healthy and stiff cells as dead. The parasite then replicates asexually for about 48 hours, dividing inside the red blood cell until it’s so full of Plasmodium that it bursts. Like house flippers, the parasites move on to other blood cells. Within days, millions could be lurking in the bloodstream. In this way, malaria can quickly overwhelm a human host. It is all enabled by the moving junction that allows the parasites to set up shop without tipping off the authorities. The structure of the moving junction could help researchers intervene, with drugs to block the parasite from invading a host blood cell in the first place. Moving Target Malaria treatment has long been something of a hit-or-miss proposition. Without a granular view of how Plasmodium interacts with host cells, researchers had to test various compounds by trial and error. If a given drug seemed to fight the illness, they had little idea what part of the infection process it had disrupted. “All that work was done essentially blind,” Deitsch said. This has made developing new malaria treatments notoriously difficult. The former workhorse antimalarial drugs, such as chloroquine, sulfadoxine, and pyrimethamine, are now known to target the parasites in the bloodstream. But the Plasmodium species that infect humans are rapidly evolving resistance to these compounds . Invasion offers a tantalizing choke point for new medicines. “If you block invasion, then you stop the parasite in its tracks,” Ho said. To make her point, her team used an AI-powered protein-design platform to craft an inhibitory protein that could block the moving junction. In test tubes, it prevented Plasmodium from entering red blood cells. But its safety and efficacy haven’t been tested in animal models. It’s possible that the moving junction could be something of a skeleton key that could be used to treat other parasitic diseases. Plasmodium is a member of the apicomplexans, a large phylum of parasitic protists that also includes Toxoplasma gondii , a cat parasite, and Cyclospora , which causes explosive diarrhea. These single-celled organisms appear to enter using the same biochemical equipment as Plasmodium . “All of these are parasites that have this invasion machinery,” Deitsch said. The study of those conditions could in turn inform malaria treatment. A 2026 paper described the mechanism by which Toxoplasma senses the right moment to deploy its moving junction, and malaria may operate the same way. But the moving junction may prove to be too much of a moving target. “Some people have always argued that invasion is a really bad drug target because it’s a very short process,” van Ooij said. Any drug with the ability to stop invasion would have a roughly 60-second window in which to do so, which means it would need to remain stable in the body for a long time or act extremely quickly, or both. Ho’s team already has their sights set on another target. They plan to use similar cryo-electron microscopy techniques to solve the structure of other protein complexes involved in malaria infection, such as those adhesive proteins that keep infected blood cells from journeying to the spleen. “We’ve caught one white whale,” Ho said. “So we want to go after the other remaining white whales.” Editor’s note: This research was funded in part by the Simons Foundation, which also funds this editorially independent magazine . Simons Foundation funding decisions have no influence on our coverage. articles.title: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins
articles.summary: AI design tools make proteins that break bonds that are stable for hundreds of years.
articles.content: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins - Ars Technica Skip to content Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they’re estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth’s environment, most proteins don’t last nearly that long. That’s because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment. Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases. Cutting proteins The basic peptide bond isn’t especially interesting-looking—it’s what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.) Peptide bonds are formed by the removal of a water molecule from parts of an amino group and an acidic group. Credit: Wikimedia Commons Peptide bonds are formed by the removal of a water molecule from parts of an amino group and an acidic group. Credit: Wikimedia Commons Breaking these bonds apart simply reverses the process by breaking apart the peptide bond and a water molecule, and linking their parts. Because both components are chemically stable, the reaction requires an enzyme to occur with any frequency. Without an enzyme, a typical peptide bond would be stable for hundreds of years in water. Life has evolved a handful of enzyme mechanisms that manage this catalysis. The research at issue here relied on two different ones. One is a zinc protease , where the positive charge of the zinc atom coordinates the peptide bond that’s being broken, key parts of the protease, and a water molecule. The protease partially pulls a proton off the water molecule, activating it to attack and break up the peptide bond. The second protease the researchers use is called a cysteine protease . In this case, a cysteine (one of the amino acids) in the enzyme is activated to attack the peptide bond, creating a temporary intermediate where part of the protein being cut is chemically linked to the enzyme. A water molecule eventually breaks this intermediate apart, releasing the second part of the cut protein. Both of these mechanisms require a handful of specific amino acids from the protease to be located in close proximity within the catalytic center of the protease. Other amino acids in the protease help ensure these key catalytic amino acids are brought together in the right place with the right orientation. The rest of the protease may also enforce a degree of specificity on what proteins get cut. Some proteases, like the ones active in our digestive system, can make cuts next to any amino acid. Others are slightly more selective, preferring to cut near positively or negatively charged amino acids. And a few are very highly specific, such as the protease that activates insulin, which only cuts near a very specific series of amino acids. Designer enzymes The people behind the new work, primarily from Nobel-winner David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, viewed designing a protease as a challenge. For one, the stability of the peptide bonds means that reactions wouldn’t take place without an effective catalyst. And to get that catalyst requires an extremely precise arrangement of specific amino acids. So it wasn’t obvious that the AI protein design tools the lab developed were up to the task. Both projects took a similar approach. Just like evolution, they started with an existing protease. One was a zinc protease used in a crayfish’s digestive system. The other was a cysteine protease from yeast. In both cases, the protein structure was known, as were the key amino acids that catalyze cleaving other proteins. The design process started with these amino acids. The design process started with software called RFdiffusion2, which creates a backbone for the enzyme (the backbone consists of the protein’s repeated peptide bonds). The researchers gave RFdiffusion2 a number of constraints. To start, any backbone it designed had to bring together the key catalytic amino acids needed for a functional protease. They also gave it a target amino acid sequence where the protease would eventually cut. The backbone had to accommodate that target sequence in close proximity to the catalytic center. With a backbone laid out, the process next moved to ProteinMPNN, a tool that works along the backbone, populating it with specific amino acids. (That tool featured in Google’s efforts to watermark AI-designed proteins.) ProteinMPNN selects each amino acid based on a series of constraints. For starters, the amino acid must be compatible with the backbone folding up into its planned structure. Next, in critical areas, each amino acid chosen needs to be compatible with the formation of the enzyme’s catalytic site. And finally, in nearby areas, it has to be compatible with latching on to the intended target. The researchers repeated this process dozens of times for both the cysteine and zinc proteases. For the cysteine protease, they made 12 different backbones and populated them with 69 different sets of amino acids. For the zinc project, they tried 135 different protein designs. They used AlphaFold3 to predict the structures of many of these designs and found nothing in the databases that looked much like them, confirming their tools weren’t simply stealing previously identified structures. Do they work? The researchers started by making a single, long protein that contained the protease, the sequence it was designed to target, and a fluorescent protein. They then tested to see if the fluorescent protein was cut loose. In the case of the cysteine protease, they got 13 designs that worked, a success rate of 19 percent, although all of them were considerably less active than the yeast enzyme that was used as a model. The zinc project was a bit more complicated. They tested many designs that didn’t include the water molecule that normally takes part in that reaction. These had a relatively low success rate, with only 14 out of 89 showing weak catalytic activity. When they modeled the ones that didn’t work, they found that the designs often let a water molecule block the site where reactions should take place. So, they also tried designs where they placed a water molecule in the right location as an additional design constraint. These had a much higher success rate, with 35 out of 38 showing some catalytic activity. Again, however, their activity was considerably lower than the enzyme that was used as the starting point for the designs. (They did get one design with a better level of activity, but it wasn’t specific about where it cut other proteins.) To find out whether this activity could be improved, the researchers identified amino acids that were in close proximity to the active site of the protease, but not actively involved with the catalysis. And they swapped in every alternative amino acid that wasn’t predicted to disrupt the structure of the design. They found some versions that were considerably more active; the best version they identified accelerated the cleavage of the peptide bond by a factor of 10 9 while remaining highly specific for the intended target protein sequence. Similar things happened with the zinc-based protease. Their v2 version of their protease, which incorporated some of the random mutations, was 30 times more active than the original design it was based on. It also accelerated peptide-bond cleavage by a factor of 10 10 . As a final demonstration of this approach’s promise, the researchers designed zinc proteases that could target proteins associated with neurological disorders, such as Alzheimer’s and frontotemporal dementia. Attempting to modify their existing design to target a new sequence didn’t work well, so they started the process over from the start and managed to find something that could cut the intended target in cells. For the researchers, this suggests that we might ultimately be able to influence the course of some genetic diseases by targeting the malformed proteins that cause them. What do the results tell us? The potential therapeutic use of this is complicated. Proteins are often difficult to deliver to the site where they’re needed, and can often trigger an immune response. Things get even more challenging if the protease target is inside a cell rather than on the exterior. That would likely require the target cells to make the protease, which would involve delivering the gene encoding it to the cells where it’s needed. So, there are considerable hurdles that would need to be cleared before we could potentially start developing therapies using this technology. The researchers also highlight how the work shows some limitations of the tools. As used, they successfully designed proteins that matched all the physical constraints they were given: They folded up into structures that brought the amino acids needed to catalyze a reaction into roughly the right location, and latched on to specific target amino acid sequences. But we don’t, at the moment, have the ability to tell these tools we want any specific catalytic activity. So many designs lacked some of the subtle details that make evolved enzymes such great catalysts. In other words, the tools are great at structure, but they’re not necessarily great at activity. And, while structure is essential for function, it isn’t everything. As the researchers saw, introducing random mutation could still make subtle structural tweaks that produced enzymes that were considerably more active. Of course, this protein design software is only a few years old, and both developers and users might have ideas for incorporating constraints beyond physical location. Nature, 2026. articles.title: How Do Fungi Keep the Planet Healthy?
articles.summary: Evolutionary biologist Toby Kiers explains how fungal networks in soil trade nutrients with plants, help keep carbon underground, and strike bargains without having a brain. The post How Do Fungi Keep the Planet Healthy? first appeared on Quanta Magazine
articles.content: How Do Fungi Keep the Planet Healthy? | Quanta Magazine Home How Do Fungi Keep the Planet Healthy? Read Later Share Copied! Comments Read Later Read Later The Joy of Why How Do Fungi Keep the Planet Healthy? By Steven Strogatz and Janna Levin October 15, 2026 Evolutionary biologist Toby Kiers explains how fungal networks in soil trade nutrients with plants, help keep carbon underground, and strike bargains without having a brain. Read Later Chanelle Nibbelink for Quanta Magazine Introduction People may think of soil as just dirt, but it is anything but inert. Beneath your feet, a vast network of mycorrhizal fungi is hard at work, trading minerals with plant roots. This trading system helps enrich the soil, and it sequesters 13 billion tons of atmospheric carbon dioxide each year — roughly equivalent to one-third of the world’s fossil-fuel emissions. Scientists know that these fungi form partnerships with 80% of all plant species on Earth, a relationship that evolved some 450 million years ago. What they have not understood is how organisms with no brain or central nervous system can decide whom to trade with, and on what terms. Toby Kiers, an evolutionary biologist at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, has spent much of her career making this hidden world visible. Drawing on economics and game theory, and using tools that range from fluorescent quantum dots to imaging robots, her lab is probing how fungi and plants conduct their trade. The work raises new questions about soil, carbon, and even what counts as an individual organism. In this episode, Kiers tells co-host Steven Strogatz how these brainless, decentralized organisms can behave strategically — discriminating between better and worse partners and shifting resources across the network to wherever a plant will “pay” more for it — and how she has built a worldwide community of researchers to map the biodiversity of these underground networks and advocate for their protection. Listen on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , TuneIn or your favorite podcasting app, or you can stream it from Quanta . Transcript [ Music plays ] STEVE STROGATZ: I’m Steve Strogatz. JANNA LEVIN: And I’m Janna Levin. STROGATZ: And this is The Joy of Why. LEVIN: A podcast from Quanta Magazine where we explore some of the biggest unanswered questions in math and science today. STROGATZ: Hey there, Janna. I would love to talk to you about a big question. LEVIN: Okay. STROGATZ: Imagine you’re walking around in the forest or in Central Park. LEVIN: That’s my forest! STROGATZ: I know, so what’s under your feet? What are your shoes hitting? LEVIN: I think people would be very surprised that there’s real nature in Central Park. So you got the grass, you got the trees. Uh, there’s dirt. We have birds. STROGATZ: Let’s focus on the dirt. LEVIN: Is dirt our topic today? STROGATZ: Dirt is related to our topic. We wanna talk about what’s happening underground in the form of what are called mycorrhizal fungi. I learned that I’m supposed to say fun-gee. LEVIN: Not fun-guy? STROGATZ: Not fun-guy. LEVIN: I say fun- fung- fun-guy. STROGATZ: Well, what would I say? I would probably s- I don’t know. Fun-ji? LEVIN: So now I have to say fun-gee? STROGATZ: You’re supposed to say fun-gee for the purpose of this episode. LEVIN: Is that like saying Uranus? STROGATZ: [ Laughs ] You should be saying that. LEVIN: I do yeah. STROGATZ: Well, so I spoke to someone recently that changed my perspective about these fungi under our feet and the wood wide web. Not the worldwide web, the wood wide web. It’s the mycorrhizal network of these vast networks of fungi that we never notice that are underground, and they’re incredibly important in connecting the roots and supplying nutrients to trees and other plants. Something like 80% to 90% of all the plant species all over the world are getting help from these fungi. They’re also helping our atmosphere and our climate. They enrich the soil to help farmers and biodiversity, agriculture. They may even contribute to cloud formation through the release of their spores over rainforests. LEVIN: Wow. STROGATZ: So they may not get much respect, the fungi, but they’re right up there with the animals and plants in mattering to the world. LEVIN: Yeah, ’cause you always hear about the role of bacteria, and so it’s really interesting how fungi could affect the whole ecosystem like that. STROGATZ: Well, the bacteria are very intimately associated with these fungi. and That’s something that we’re going to hear from our guest about. LEVIN: Alright. STROGATZ: Toby Kiers is her name. She is an evolutionary biologist at the Vrije University in Amsterdam, and a recent MacArthur Fellow. So if you’re ready, here we go. [ Music plays ] STROGATZ: Welcome to The Joy of Why , Toby. TOBY KIERS: Thanks so much about having me. STROGATZ: Well, this is an area that is not familiar to me at all, and I’m dying to hear about it. Can you describe what your subject area is first, just in very broad terms? KIERS: I study the class of organisms called mycorrhizal fungi, and the word mycorrhizal means myco , which means fungus, and rhizal , which means root. So these are a class of fungi that form a very intimate association with the vast majority of plants. So over 80% of all plant species on Earth form these partnerships, and it’s a very old partnership. It evolved some 450 million years ago, and was actually really fundamental for plants that were in a wet, aquatic environment to start colonizing land hundreds of millions of years ago. And since then, it’s been an incredibly important relationship in building ecosystems that we live and survive on today. And I don’t think many people know, but actually the fungus served as a plant root system for even tens of millions of years. Roots are kind of a new evolutionary innovation, so it’s a very intimate and old partnership between plants and fungi. STROGATZ: So you’re saying the plants didn’t go to the bother of making their own roots? They were somehow using the fungi to do that for them? KIERS: Exactly. So, what the plants were doing was they were sending carbon that they were photosynthesizing and taking out of the atmosphere and feeding it to these loose associations, these fungal networks that were in the soil, and in return they were getting resources like phosphorus and nitrogen. See, the thing that fungi are very good at is breaking up rocks and digesting these hard-to-access minerals. And so they were feeding it to the plants, and in return the plants were giving carbon. And now this partnership really underlies our ecosystems on Earth. STROGATZ: Oh, wow. I have all kinds of questions. First of all, very dramatic to say breaking up rocks. I don’t, just haven’t thought about it. What are they doing to break up rocks? KIERS: Well, the fungi make these beautiful complex networks, and fungi are very good at digesting outside of their bodies and actually partnering with other microbes like bacteria that can help break down rocks. So, some people even say they’re very good at eating rocks on the outside of their bodies and having it dissolve into a form that can then be taken up. And so the fungi then take up these nutrients and move them through these vast networks and feed them to plant roots. And in return —obviously they don’t do this for free — the plants are feeding them a diet of sugar and lipids like fats. It’s like the most brilliant diet of sugar and fats that is provided by the plants to the fungi. And this partnership is very common. It’s almost ubiquitous, I would say, across terrestrial ecosystems. And because of this partnership and because plants are constantly feeding carbon down to these networks, we actually call it one of Earth’s circulatory systems. STROGATZ: Oh, nice. So, network is a word that everybody is using these days. We hear about the internet. We know we have our own circulatory system in our body, networks of blood vessels. But so when you talk about a mycorrhizal fungal network, what should I picture? KIERS: Exactly. And it’s very clear. One thing I really want people to understand is that plants are not fungi , and fungi are not plants, and they’re very different kingdoms of life. So when you have a plant root and you were to pull it up from the ground, that’s a beautiful image, you would not quite be able to see these threads that are hanging from the root. Absolutely incredible ecosystems with really high diversity, and also some of what we think are the most dense arbuscular mycorrhizal networks on Earth is in this area. And in all cases, what we do is we work with local collaborators who have very specific questions about the ecosystems, and actually go out and use a grid system to take soil samples, and actually pound a core into the earth and extract that core and bring the soil back to a lab, extract the fungal DNA, and start sequencing these communities. STROGATZ: So you’re sequencing them. Do you just wanna have a taxonomy of the kind of diversity out there? Or what is the question? KIERS: Yeah, well, I think like a decade ago creating a blueprint of Earth’s living underground fungal networks would’ve seemed impossible, right? I think like historically, we understand the patterns of forests across the Earth. We understand ocean patterns. I mean, really our tools have been confined to what’s happening at the Earth’s surface. But now we’ve got these amazing emerging techniques in remote sensing, in machine learning, in fungal sequencing, and in robotics that we can actually start to understand what’s happening underground. And by doing that, we’re learning how fungi can be leveraged to restore degraded lands, to increase agricultural sustainability, to draw down carbon. There’s so many. Even trying to go to these places where there’s pollution and understand what fungal communities are there, and what is it about their… what is it in their genomes that allow them to break down pollutants? So many questions that we can ask with these data sets. STROGATZ: I’m getting the feeling listening to you that sort of like when people began to explore the oceans wondering what’s there. You know, it’s just a very simple kind of question. We don’t even know what’s out there. It feels like that’s what’s animating some of this, that there’s a vast unexplored terra incognita that happens to be subterranean. KIERS: Not only is that animating it, but fungi are the most charismatic and fun-to-work-with organisms. So there’s this real passion of mycologists all over the world that have been so underfunded and so marginalized in many ways because it wasn’t even until sort of the 1970s, late ‘60s I think, that fungi were recognized as their own kingdom. I mean, before they were just placed in with plants. And so it’s really shining a light on the underdog of biological diversity. And so what we’re doing now is working with all these data sets and all of these scientists all over the world. I think now there’s about 600 SPUN associates in, like, over 80 countries, and we’re working together to create something called the Underground Atlas. And that’s this digital tool that allows decision-makers to actually start quantifying and tracking and protecting hidden underground fungal communities. We’re asking, where’s the Amazon of the underground? Is it in the Amazon? Like, where are these hotspots of biodiversity, and are they being protected? So I think it was in last year, in 2025, we had a big paper in Nature that showed that 90% of mycorrhizal biodiversity hotspots are outside protected areas. So only 10% of hotspots are actually inside protected areas currently. And so, we’re trying to get these maps to decision-makers and say like, “Listen, this is key biodiversity that’s been ignored for so long,” and it’s also a library of solutions to really important questions facing the world in terms of, like, how are we gonna restore degraded lands? Like you need these fungal networks to jumpstart those soil systems, but what if all of those local habitats, the fungal refugia that are so key, and those strains, those, the, all that biodiversity is lost? How are you going to start to restore an underground ecosystem? STROGATZ: Let me follow up on a few very striking things you said, so many really. The use of the word “charismatic” is one of them. I think you’ve made the case for some of the charismatic features of fungi, but I wonder if you have more that you didn’t have a chance to mention yet? KIERS: Well, we use beautiful techniques, for example, confocal microscopy to look into these organisms. If you were to zoom in and actually look at the spores of these organisms, they contain hundreds of nuclei that shine like little bright stars inside a balloon, and they’re the most incredible structures that you’ve ever seen. And to think that these spores are traveling through the air and actually changing our weather patterns, right? I mean, more and more we’re starting to understand how spores, fungal spores in the air, are an important input to generate clouds over rainforests. What is not charismatic about that? They’re so beautiful on a small microscopic level, and then up in the atmosphere they’re floating around forming clouds. I mean, there’s just nothing quite like it. STROGATZ: Great. As we come towards the end of our conversation, I’d like to sort of pan back even further now to talk to you about some big questions about life, interdependence, intelligence, evolution, things like that. I get the feeling that your work challenges a lot of the usual binaries about individuals versus networks or cooperation versus competition or organism versus ecosystem. Do fungi force us to rethink what a living system is? KIERS: I think fungi really challenge so much of what we think we know about the living world. They challenge our understanding of sex. They challenge our understanding of defining what is an individual. They challenge our understanding of how something so small can have such magnitudes of effects at the global level, even though it’s such a small microbe, it’s almost invisible. And I think that’s what makes it so interesting to work with is that every day when you’re working with mycorrhizal fungi, you’re challenged. They make it so you never know what’s going to happen in a given experiment. They keep you guessing. We call them divas sometimes, in the nicest way possible, because they keep us coming back, because they open up this idea of curiosity-driven science. You know how, we ask this question in the lab, “What is it like to be you?” We’re asking the fungi, “What is it like to be you?” And I think it’s a very respectful question because it allows them to be them and for us to be on the sidelines to develop tools to actually try to understand their inner lives. So, when we talk about things like economics and using different terminologies, it’s just asking questions in a different way and taking the time to understand how these organisms live so differently in the world. STROGATZ: Uh-huh. Okay. Well, I can’t leave you without hearing more about… How did you put it? They’re forcing us to redefine what we mean by sex or something like that? KIERS: Yeah, they’re challenging our understanding of sex. So mycorrhizal fungi, these arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi in particular, are a great example. There’s work coming out of our group here in Amsterdam led by Vasilis Kokkoris, who’s an incredible geneticist in many ways studying mycorrhizal fungi. And he studies that there are two genomes simultaneously inside a single network. So it’s, imagine our human body, but instead of having one genome, it has two genomes inside the same, what we would think of as an individual. It just doesn’t make any sense, and so he’s starting to understand, is there a cooperation between these two genomes? Who gets to colonize what parts of the network? Is an individual even a network, or is an individual just a genome, tiny little nuclei floating inside this tube? It just, it’s really hard to understand. And then we don’t even know, do these genomes, do they recombine? For, for many years, the conventional idea is that these are asexual organisms, yet we see hints that maybe there’s a different kind of sex going on. So lots of open questions about how these fungi just reproduce. We know they make spores. We know these spores go into the air. We know that the spores germinate and make what you would think is a new individual. But because there’s hundreds of nuclei inside a spore, and they’re not all the same, it just doesn’t make much sense using our conventional understanding of genetics. STROGATZ: Hmm. They seem to be real champions of living in an interdependent way, even across kingdoms. I mean, we could do well to learn from them. I don’t know. Do you have thoughts about this? Is nature more cooperative? Are they a paradigm of what cooperation can look like even when you’re looking out for number one? KIERS: With mycorrhizal fungi, we see them as both like a physical scaffold that holds everything together, and that really drives home this idea of interdependence, right? So many organisms are built upon this scaffold of life. But there’s also this beautiful chemical interdependence, right? They’re moving carbon through the system, and fungi are collecting phosphorus and nitrogen, and there’s this beautiful sort of dependence and movement of resources. And it’s almost like this nested interaction of just so many organisms layered on. Even in the networks themselves, there can be organelles that used to be free-living bacteria inside the networks themselves. So, I think the more we look, the more interdependence and nestedness we see. Now, that doesn’t mean there’s no tension, right? There’s always a tension. It’s a beautiful tension between organisms because they have different needs. They have different resources that they need to access, to reproduce, and that creates a beautiful opera of interactions that’s not always beneficial, not always cooperative, but instead it creates a beautiful tension, very much like an opera, where sometimes the characters are getting along, and sometimes they’re not. STROGATZ: I really like your analogy there because it is operatic in that, this traditional framing, or at least very commonplace about selfishness, puts such a negative tone on the thing, whereas when you speak of it as opera or drama, it’s like each character has desires. It needs certain things. It wants what it wants, and that’s not exactly selfish. It’s just, it’s the nature of being alive. We all have our needs. KIERS: Exactly. And I just don’t think that we should be scared of studying that tension in a curious way because that tension leads to innovation, right? When there’s some kind of conflict between organisms, that leads to the generation of new ideas. And that’s always really interesting is that it’s not s- everybody thinks that conflict in and of itself or that tension is a bad thing, but actually can generate biological diversity and allow organisms to create ecosystems that are much more complex than they would be otherwise. STROGATZ: That’s beautiful. Well, you really give the impression of someone having fun being a scientist. KIERS: Yes, lots of fun and very little sleep ’cause there’s a lot to do. There’s a lot to do. STROGATZ: All right. Well, thank you very much, Toby. This has been great fun for us too. We’re really happy to have you on The Joy of Why . KIERS: It was so fun. Thanks so much for having me. [ Music plays ] LEVIN: It’s so interesting to imagine organisms interacting competitively, operatically. I love that image. But also beyond co-dependence, I mean, there are bacterial organelles that have been synthesized into fungi. That seems like the boundary between separate organisms has also diffused, and that’s pretty remarkable. There also seems to be this kind of, like, evolutionary idea that pressure creates evolution. It drives evolution, right? STROGATZ: Yeah, that’s right. We do use that phrase, right? Selective pressure. We tend to think, oh, stress is a bad thing. We need to reduce stress in our lives or conflict, and I think it’s an interesting instructive point that Toby makes that, yes, of course, you don’t wanna overdo it with stress and tension and all that, but a certain amount of tension or stress or competition can lead to complexity, she mentions, innovation. It does appear to be very deeply woven into the nature of life. LEVIN: Yeah, I feel like there’s also a metaphor for life there somehow. You know, how to take lessons from nature and how to evolve. STROGATZ: Anyway, we don’t have much choice. That does seem to be the way things are. LEVIN: So these fungi are really so interconnected and so interdependent that, do they talk about that boundary of organisms where they have really begun to merge to some extent? STROGATZ: Yeah, it’s very tricky to think about what’s an organism, what’s a system, an ecosystem, a population, a colony. It’s an issue we’ve gotten into with some of our other guests in The Joy of Why. It’s really maybe a case where our human-imposed distinctions may not line up very well with the way nature operates. We’re putting categories on things that are just more subtle than that. LEVIN: I wonder if people are also thinking about ways to induce these networks to help clean up some of the climate crisis that we’re facing. If these are so influential and they have such an important role in terms of, if you like, the economics of the ecosystem or the economics of the biosphere, is there a way that we can guide a fungi to help clean up this mess? STROGATZ: Hmm. You know, I don’t know that they need any encouragement from us. They just need protection to not have their ecosystems devastated. And, she did mention that a vast amount of these mycorrhizal networks are not the places being protected. LEVIN: Wow, right. STROGATZ: So, this is what she and her colleagues are trying to bring attention to. Because we don’t see them, we don’t notice or think about them but they may be just as important. LEVIN: Yeah. Maybe nature will show us the way. STROGATZ: Yeah. As always, it’s been a pleasure. LEVIN: Thank you, Steve. STROGATZ: See you next time. [ Music plays ] LEVIN: If you’re enjoying The Joy of Why and you’re not already subscribed, hit the subscribe or follow button wherever you’re listening. You can also leave a review for the show. It helps people find this podcast. Find articles, newsletters, videos and more at quantamagazine.org. articles.title: A 1,000-mile cloud on Mars may reveal physics never seen in nature
articles.summary: A new model suggests Mars may host ice-forming physics never directly observed before.
articles.content: A 1,000-mile cloud on Mars may reveal physics never seen in nature - Ars Technica Skip to content Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav Every morning during the Martian spring and summer, a thin and extremely long cloud emerges, only to disappear again. The wispy formation appears near the volcano Arsia Mons and gradually elongates until it reaches over 1,000 miles—about the distance from New York to Kansas City as the crow flies—before dissipating. This cycle then repeats for several months. Since it was first recorded by a probe in 2018, scientists have been unable to find a plausible explanation for the existence of this cloud, often referred to as the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC). Until now. Recently, researchers successfully modeled the cloud’s formation for the first time, their results suggesting that it may be driven by a physical process that has never been directly observed in any planet’s atmosphere. “We found that we needed to include some exotic physics… physics that, while included in textbooks, is treated as theoretical and usually thought not to happen in nature. It certainly hasn’t been seen in action before,” Jorge Hernández-Bernal, a planetary scientist at Paris’ Sorbonne Université and lead author of the study, said in a press release . “Once we included this physics in our simulations, the AMEC emerged just as we hoped.” On Earth, clouds usually form when water vapor creates droplets or ice crystals in the presence of tiny particles, such as dust or salt. The new study, published in Nature Geoscience , instead suggests AMEC could be forming through so-called homogeneous nucleation, where vapor changes directly into ice crystals on its own without any help from debris. “It’s akin to droplets of condensation appearing in the middle of a room, rather than on a window,” Hernández-Bernal explained. “It’s wholly unexpected.” This phenomenon requires extreme conditions—a sharp temperature drop of 30° Celsius within 10 minutes and high relative humidity. The Arsia Mons volcano also plays a key role. When wind current hits the 65,000-foot-tall volcano , it creates a powerful wave that launches moist air high in the atmosphere in a matter of minutes. Scientists have assumed a similar phenomenon could occur in the upper atmospheres of other planets, including Venus and even Earth, but it has never been observed . That’s not too surprising given the extreme air humidity required for this phenomenon, which is more than 100,000 times greater than any value measured on Earth. Before this modeling, it was not known that these humidity levels existed on Mars either. “We don’t have nearly as much information about Mars’ atmosphere as we do about Earth’s, so reproducing the AMEC to this degree is a big success,” said Hernández-Bernal, adding, “the result is remarkable.” This story originally appeared on WIRED Czech Republic and Slovakia and has been translated from Czech. Copy link Facebook X Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The child was buried alongside two ceramic objects depicting defeated warriors about to be sacrificed. (Image credit: Huacas de Moche Archaeological Project - UNT) Archaeologists in Peru have found an elaborate 1,500-year-old tomb that may hold the remains of a high-status toddler from a pre-Inca civilization. The burial, which is from the Moche culture, also contained vessels depicting prisoners with rope around each of their necks and a sculpture of a human-bird deity. Moche (also known as Mochica) culture developed along the northern coast of what is now Peru from the third to the ninth century . They created agricultural lands in the region's desert landscape, and their archaeological record includes monumental temples, water canals, pottery, metallurgy, textiles and a distinctive form of art. The Moche didn't have a written language, but they left behind thousands of realistic portrait vessels , which are somewhat similar to the prisoner sculptors found in the toddler's burial. Latest Videos From Live Science Watch full video here: In the newfound tomb, the team unearthed a small skeleton, which is likely the remains of a toddler who was, at most, 2 years old, Carlos Rengifo-Chunga , director of the University of Trujillo's Huacas de Moche Archaeological Project, told Live Science. The child's sex is unknown . The child was buried alongside 32 ceramic objects associated with Moche culture. (Image credit: Huacas de Moche Archaeological Project - UNT) Rengifo-Chunga and his colleagues also found two copper objects in the burial: a mask-like disk covering the child's face, and a half-moon object on their feet. In addition, the burial contained 32 ceramic objects associated with Moche culture, including those depicting the prisoners and the deity. The tomb was large compared to the child's small size, and could have easily held an adult, Rengifo-Chunga said. It dates to the sixth or seventh century, he added. The team unearthed the tomb inside the Uhle Platform at the Huacas de Moche archaeological site in northern Peru. The Uhle Platform is a mausoleum, attached to the Huaca de la Luna temple, with a patio archaeologists call the Patio of the Serpents. Of the more than 80 burials previously uncovered there, the tomb represents the only known child to receive this sort of lavish burial. Sign up for the Live Science daily newsletter now Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox. Contact me with news and offers from other Future brands Receive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsors The elaborate funerary treatment, including the use of copper, and the location of the tomb all suggest that the child belonged to an elite class of Moche society, Rengifo-Chunga said. The two prisoner sculptures are associated with the "ritual of combat," a common theme in Moche art. In this sort of imagery, two warriors fight each other, and the loser is stripped of his clothes and weapons, tied around the neck with a rope and offered as a human sacrifice, Rengifo-Chunga said. The prisoners depicted on these two vessels were the losing warriors, and their presence in the burial of a child is rare. "One would normally presume that these kinds of vessels represent something related to the deceased's life," Rengifo-Chunga said. For example, a vessel like this might signify that the individual took part in combat. Image 1 of 3 (Image credit: Huacas de Moche Archaeological Project - UNT) One of the ceramic objects depicts a presumed deity with human and bird features. (Image credit: Huacas de Moche Archaeological Project - UNT) An archaeological team discovered a likely elite child burial at the Huacas de Moche archaeological site in Peru. (Image credit: Huacas de Moche Archaeological Project - UNT) One of the two ceramics depicting prisoners that archaeologists found in the toddler's burial. Image 1 of 3 View Original Image 2 of 3 View Original Image 3 of 3 View Original But a toddler couldn't have taken part in such an activity. In general, archaeologists wouldn't expect to see elements of an adult ritual in the burial of a child. "This expands our knowledge on Moche funerary practices," he added. The sculpture of the presumed deity depicts a human body with bird wings and a bird tail, although for some scholars it might be interpreted as a god in transformation, Rengifo-Chunga said. The deity holds a square shield in one hand and a goblet in the other, and is flanked by two bird "assistants" wearing ceremonial garments. Related Stories 1,300-year-old throne room of powerful Moche queen discovered in Peru Decapitator nose ornament: 1,500-year-old gold jewelry depicting a bloodthirsty South American god 1,500-year-old tomb in Peru holds human sacrifices, including strangled son next to father's remains, genetic analysis reveals Researchers will have to investigate whether the deity is a known Moche god, or a newfound addition to the pantheon. Either way, the object joins a contentious debate over whether the Moche pantheon consists of many gods, or just a few that can transform into many different versions, Rengifo-Chunga said. The artifacts are now in the laboratories of the Santiago Uceda Castillo Museum in Peru, where they will undergo conservation treatment. She earned her BA from Boston College in English literature, ancient history and French, and her journalism MA from L'École Du Journalisme de Nice in International New Media Journalism. articles.title: UN says we're going to blow past 1.5º warming, offers a "now what?" answer
articles.summary: Best case is now an overshoot to 1.8o C, accompanied by massive carbon removal.
articles.content: UN says we're going to blow past 1.5º warming, offers a "now what?" answer - Ars Technica Skip to content Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav In 2015, all but two countries agreed to make an effort to keep global temperatures from reaching 1.5° C above pre-industrial readings. Since then, most of the world has largely treated what they signed on to as aspirational, and one of the largest emitters (the US) has alternately withdrawn and recommitted to the agreement. Meanwhile, the planet has responded as expected to steadily rising carbon emissions and appears to be practically at the 1.5° limit. On Wednesday, for the first time, the United Nations Environmental Programme (UNEP) acknowledged that reality and conceded that the goal of keeping warming below 1.5° was no longer a viable one. Instead, its new goalposts focus on keeping both how long we exceed that limit and how much we exceed it by, at a minimum. Doing that will require both dramatic emissions cuts now and the removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere before the century is out. Bowing to the inevitable Depending on which baseline you use to establish pre-industrial temperatures, as well as which reconstruction of global temperatures you rely on, the world has either gotten very close to, or already exceeded, the 1.5° milestone. The current El Niño event, which appears exceptionally strong, will almost certainly mean that we’ve gone over it no matter which records you choose. The UN relies on temperatures averaged over a few decades to determine where we are, which means we have technically not gone above the limit yet. But, as temperatures seem stubbornly disinterested in dropping much even after extremely hot years, we’re likely at the start of the period where the 1.5° goal is passed. So, while it’s not technically too late to get on a pathway that keeps us below this, practically it’s already too late. UNEP’s acknowledgment of this reality is straightforward, albeit couched in a bit of optimism. “Decades of insufficient climate action makes exceedance of 1.5° C unavoidable,” its latest report states. “Whether it will be temporary crucially depends on decisions taken today.” In other words, we might be committed to exceeding the goal, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that we’re accepting that global temperatures will need to stay above the 1.5° C mark. The Paris Agreement’s means of getting to that goal was to have its signatories set emissions-reduction targets and then progressively expand those as policy tools and technology matured. Progress would be measured at key points through a “stocktake” process. But not a lot of countries followed up on what they agreed to. “While the year 2030 is drawing closer, collectively countries have still not aligned policies with [agreed to] targets,” UNEP concedes. In fact, the gap between targets and actual policy would look even worse if the US were still part of the process, instead of seeing the Trump administration pull out of the agreement a second time. A decade into the process, the needed tightening of policies has also been insufficient. In its new analysis, UNEP highlights that existing policies would likely leave us at 2.8° C above preindustrial temperatures by the end of the century, while even the stretch goals under the Paris Agreement would drop that by just 0.2°. Many countries have set net-zero goals outside of the Paris Framework, but including all of those would still leave us at 2.1° C above preindustrial temperatures by the century’s end. In all of these scenarios, temperatures would continue to rise in the ensuing century. And we don’t seem to be closer to getting our act together. Emissions were largely flat between 2024 and 2025 (there appears to be a slight decline, but within uncertainties of zero change), and emissions from burning fossil fuels were actually up, offset by better land-use management. But to have reached any significant goals, they needed to be dropping by now. What’s next? But UNEP is a rare organization, in that it’s willing to say the worst is not necessarily yet to come. “Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5° C raises the risk of irreversible changes including in ice sheets, permafrost carbon, ocean circulation and coral systems, along with devastating human impacts,” the report says. “The task now, therefore, is not only to ensure that global warming stays well below 2°C, but to minimize the duration and magnitude of overshoot and establish a credible return path to 1.5° C by the end of the century.” The scenario it lays out has a 66 percent chance of keeping warming to a maximum of 1.8° C above preindustrial temperatures, and to have even odds that we can have temperatures back down below 1.5° by the century’s end. The first thing that should be obvious is that this would require removing some of the emissions we are presently placing in the atmosphere. For a technology that is still in its infancy, the goals seem extreme: 320 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide pulled out of the atmosphere by the century’s end. At the same time, that’s the rough equivalent of just over five years of present emissions pulled out over decades. But that also has to be accompanied by major emissions cuts and a transition away from fossil fuels. UNEP’s scenario would cut coal use for electricity generation by 75 percent by 2035, and phase out the fuel by 2040. All uses of oil and gas would need to be cut by 30 and 35 percent, respectively, by 2040. This is needed because greenhouse gas emissions would have to drop by 70 percent between now and 2040. Again, this highlights the insufficiency of current climate pledges. UNEP determined that these would only cut emissions by about 12 percent by 2035. Put differently, by 2035, current pledges would leave us emitting 16 gigatonnes more carbon dioxide in 2035 than we would need to stay on the minimal overshoot pathway. (The gap between pledges and needs is notably smaller in the scenario that would keep warming to 2° C by century’s end, which involves a 5 gigatonne difference.) There are failures across the board here. While coal use is declining, it’s not projected to fall nearly fast enough over the next decade. Oil and gas need to start falling, but they’re projected to rise for a decade or more. (This report would have been in preparation before the conflict with Iran disrupted oil and gas supplies, and the data on any conservation and electrification driven by shortages is not available yet.) Solar and wind are growing fast enough for a scenario that includes reasonable conservation and efficiency efforts, but because demand is rising so quickly, they’re falling behind where we need them as a percentage of the electrical grid. The report suggests we can still limit the impact of failing to meet our climate goals. But doing so will require major efforts from many countries—the same countries that got us here by not taking the initial goals seriously enough. articles.title: PHP warns it plans to release 2 emergency patches imminently
articles.summary: Unconfirmed report claims PHP2Shell exploit remotely executes code on PHP sites.
articles.content: PHP warns it plans to release 2 emergency patches imminently - Ars Technica Skip to content Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav Website admins, brace yourselves. Fixes for what are believed to be uncommonly severe vulnerabilities are scheduled to drop in a little more than 12 hours for PHP, a programming language that powers websites and Web applications everywhere. PHP maintainers said Monday that they planned to release patches for two vulnerabilities, both with severity ratings of 9.2 out of a possible 10. Waiting for PHP2Shell “All PHP users are encouraged to prepare now so they can upgrade as soon as the release is available,” the advisory stated. “We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild.” The maintainers published the advisory following the leaking of purported details, which have yet to be confirmed. The report showed a video of an exploit tool dubbed PHP2Shell executing code on webservers running: WordPress 7.1.3 MediaWiki 1.46.2 phpBB 3.3.17 Magento 2.4.9 Joomla 6.2.0 Laravel 13.36.0 Laravel 8.83.29 Symphony 8.1.9 Drupal 11.4.10 WHMCS 9.0.9 All of the above use PHP. A video depicting the tool has been reposted here . Attempts to locate the unconfirmed report were unsuccessful, but security firm watchTowr said it claimed to affect every PHP version from PHP 5, released in 2004, onward. The security firm went on to say it has confirmed that the vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are real. Researchers from another security firm, Sansec, said they “expect mass attacks to start within 15 minutes of the release.” A third security firm, Webfence, also urged admins to prepare now. Huntress has also issued an advisory. Preparation steps include identifying who is responsible for managing PHP inside an organization, taking an inventory of every app built on the language, planning a maintenance window starting at 14:00 UTC with contingency plans for moving earlier, making a backup of site and database files, and monitoring the PHP.net homepage for any late-breaking announcements, including an earlier release time. Some experts suggest unplugging any nonessential systems until they’re patched. As an open source scripting language for building dynamic websites and web apps, PHP has come to be a de facto building block for the Web. It runs multiple CMS apps in addition to WordPress and also powers many internal tools. One security researcher said an estimated 1.3 million Internet-connected hosts are likely affected. Vulnerabilities with the severity the advisories are describing have the potential to inflict major damage across the Internet. Admins should remain aware that the patches can be released at any moment and remain vigilant until they are. Update: Source file fixes were added to the php-src Github repo at 13:34 UTC this morning, with advisories here and here . Packages and docker images have begun filtering out as maintainers get their hands on the new sources. Our advice is unchanged from earlier: update as soon as possible. Dan Goodin Senior Security Editor Dan Goodin Senior Security Editor Dan Goodin is Senior Security Editor at Ars Technica, where he oversees coverage of malware, computer espionage, botnets, hardware hacking, encryption, and passwords. In his spare time, he enjoys gardening, cooking, and following the independent music scene. Dan is based in San Francisco. Follow him at here on Mastodon and here on Bluesky. articles.title: Startup taps underwater volcano as energy source in "proof point" test
articles.summary: Can undersea geothermal power help Pacific Rim nations cut down on oil imports?
articles.content: Startup taps underwater volcano as energy source in "proof point" test - Ars Technica Skip to content Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav The world’s first demonstration of a subsea geothermal power plant has taken place near an active underwater volcano almost a mile below the ocean surface. It generated less than 10 seconds of net-positive electricity but showed the technical feasibility of tapping another form of renewable energy underwater. The three-week test deployment of the 3-ton prototype power plant took place at the Axial Seamount in the northeast Pacific Ocean in September. Endurance Energy, the Seattle-based startup behind the effort, aims to eventually commercialize subsea geothermal power for Pacific island nations and other customers looking for alternatives to importing expensive fossil fuels. “The deep ocean gives us unlimited cold seawater for cooling, and its weight keeps the system and the well pressurized, so our plants can be compact,” said Andrew Redd , founder and CEO of Endurance Energy, in an email to Ars. But efforts to tap geothermal power on the seafloor face many different challenges from land-based geothermal projects, which can also add up to higher installation and operational costs. So Endurance Energy must demonstrate consistent underwater operations as well as prove the approach can be cost-effective. “It’s probably technically feasible, but it would undoubtedly be more expensive than to do it on land,” said Roland Horne , professor of energy science & engineering at Stanford University, in an emailed response to Ars. Deep sea drilling Endurance Energy’s deployment required a subsea lander drill to deploy from the ship Ocean Guardian —operated by Stabbert Maritime—and drill two holes in the seafloor at a depth of about 5,000 feet (1,524 meters). That means the test took place at a depth exceeding 2.5 times the height of the One World Trade Center building in New York City, which is the tallest building in the United States. Both the drilled holes started venting hot hydrothermal fluid measured at a temperature of about 500° F (260° C). The Endurance Energy team proceeded to case and cement the second hole before installing a valve to create a well. Next up, the company deployed its 100-kilowatt power plant, named Adélie, that is designed to vaporize incoming hydrothermal fluid to spin a turbine and drive an electric generator. It used the assistance of Canada’s remotely operated submersible ROPOS to help connect the power plant to the newly drilled well. Adélie also connected to Endurance Energy’s Seattle command center by plugging into the Regional Cabled Array , a 559-mile (900-kilometer) network of undersea fiber-optic and electric cables that provides both power and connectivity to scientific sensors on the seafloor. The undersea network is funded by the US National Science Foundation and is operated by the University of Washington. That all set the stage for the Adélie power test. But a major hitch soon arose—the drilled well extending 52 feet (16 meters) down into the seafloor was not delivering enough of the hydrothermal fluid to run the power plant. “For our first well, the goal was to show we could drill, case, cement, and cap a well on the seafloor, so we kept it small and shallow,” Redd explained. “That limited how much fluid it could deliver, and deeper wells should change that.” The test well was also just 2 inches (5 centimeters) wide, compared to oil, gas, and onshore geothermal wells that typically have casings 20 to 36 inches (51 to 91 centimeters) across. Endurance Energy plans to avoid this issue in the future by drilling deeper wells to access more fluid. The company’s current lander drill can reach about 260 feet (80 meters), which would be five times deeper than the initial test well. Powering on To try running the Adélie power plant anyway, the team redeployed it to a nearby natural vent where hydrothermal fluid was already flowing out at about 538° F (281° C). On September 27, they gave it a try. Over nearly half a minute, the power plant turbine reached about 26,000 rpm and enabled the generator to produce 60 watt-hours of electricity. The power plant also became net-positive by producing more electricity than it consumed for about 8.7 seconds. It produced a median of about 2 kilowatts of net power and peaked at 16.5 kilowatts of net power. “It’s the proof point,” Redd told Ars. “Net-positive is the threshold that matters: the plant made more power than it took to run itself on the seafloor, which no one had done before.” The 100-kilowatt power plant named Adélie was designed to tap geothermal energy from the seafloor. Credit: Endurance Energy The 100-kilowatt power plant named Adélie was designed to tap geothermal energy from the seafloor. Credit: Endurance Energy But then a software issue brought the power run to a halt. Before the generator takes over, Adélie first relies on a battery to run its pumps, thrusters, and controls, along with spinning the turbine to get it up to speed, Redd explained. A battery module recorded a brief spike in current during the spin-up process and then stopped reporting. That prompted Adélie’s software to automatically stop the power plant as a safety precaution, because it kept relying on the old reading from the battery module. When the team was restarting the power plant, a power cable feeding the refrigerant pump also failed when an imperfection in the cable casing allowed seawater to seep in and short two of the electrical conductors. That ended the trial run, although Endurance Energy already plans to use the experience to improve how it builds and tests subsea cables. Future deployments Placing the geothermal plant on top of a natural hydrothermal vent was a one-time test for purely research and demonstration purposes, Redd said. His company still plans to rely on drilled wells in future deployments. Endurance Energy also described taking steps to reduce potential environmental impacts on the seafloor and marine life. The team described choosing the “least disruptive” site for the test run and continuously monitored the process by sampling the water and recording the seafloor array of tubeworms, snails, crabs, and bacterial mats. It also checked findings against scientific sensors run by independent researchers and sent water, rock, and mineral samples for independent lab analysis. The company’s next trial run planned for the winter of 2026—2027 will involve a refurbished and upgraded Adélie—renamed Gentoo in keeping with the penguin-inspired naming—that will aim to sustain higher power generation. The company is also developing a larger 2-megawatt commercial generator for its first planned commercial deployment with the Kingdom of Tonga in 2027. The Polynesian island nation in the South Pacific Ocean runs its power grid primarily on imported diesel fuel, which has significantly increased in price since the United States and Israel launched their war with Iran . “The 2 MW commercial generators will be about the size of a shipping container, and we are deploying up to six of these generators [to] offshore Tonga,” Redd told Ars. “The physical footprint of this project will be relatively small.” Geothermal energy projects are already cost-effective on land but “on the edge of competitive pricewise,” said Horne at Stanford University. So he cautioned that any factors making geothermal more expensive would “push it to the noncompetitive side.” Still, other customers may consider Endurance Energy’s approach if the company can demonstrate reliable operations over time with the Kingdom of Tonga. The skyrocketing cost of imported fossil fuels is a huge factor that has already spurred multiple governments to invest in more renewable energy alternatives. “Large markets with ample offshore geothermal resources include the United States—Pacific Northwest and Alaska—Taiwan, and Japan,” Redd said. “As the technology matures, we expect to compete on cost and deliver continuous, weather-independent power to utilities and large energy users.” Jeremy Hsu Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu is a reporter exploring a wide range of topics across deep tech and AI. He has previously written for New Scientist, Scientific American, IEEE Spectrum, Wired, Undark Magazine and MIT Tech Review, among many other publications, about topics such as deepfakes, data centers, drones, battery tech, robotics, and GPS jamming. He also has a Master of Arts in Journalism from NYU, and a bachelor's degree from University of Pennsylvania in History and Sociology of Science, with a minor in English. 36 Comments Comments Forum view Loading comments...
