In recent decades, colorectal cancer rates have risen among young people in the U.S., although in absolute terms, the disease remains rare in this age group. (Image credit: Marco VDM via Getty Images) Copy link Facebook X Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter More children, teens and very young adults are being diagnosed with colorectal cancer in the United States, and new research suggests they often experience aggressive forms of the disease. While diagnosis rates are rising, the disease is still rare among young people. Colorectal cancer, which affects the lower intestines and rectum, is largely a disease of age: 55% of all colorectal cancers are diagnosed in people over 65, and only 16% occur in people ages 49 or younger, according to a 2026 study published in the flagship journal of the American Cancer Society . Only a few hundred cases per year are diagnosed in people under age 21 in the U.S. Nevertheless, the numbers of cases in the very young are rising, even as colorectal cancer rates decline or hold steady in older individuals. This increase coincides with an overall rise in colon and rectal cancer rates in people under 50 . The reasons for this schism aren't entirely understood. People over 50 receive routine colonoscopies in which precancerous polyps are removed, and that likely accounts for much of the decline in colorectal cancer diagnoses in older adults. But researchers suspect that environmental factors, such as ultraprocessed foods and sedentary lifestyles, might be behind the growing rates in young people. Scientists are looking to the gut microbiome for clues about why colorectal cancer is on the rise in young people. (Image credit: SEBASTIAN KAULITZKI/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY via Getty Images) "Most of the research has really focused on the gut microbiome," the community of bacteria and other microbes that live in the gut, said Dr. Christopher Lieu , a professor of medical oncology at the University of Colorado Anschutz and a medical adviser to the nonprofit Colorectal Cancer Alliance . Microbiome disruptions may spur inflammation , which, in turn, may trigger DNA mutations that cause cancer. But these mechanisms are complicated, Lieu told Live Science, and there likely isn't one simple reason young people's microbiomes may be getting disturbed. "It's going to be extraordinarily more complex than that," he said. Aggressive disease in young people What researchers are starting to learn is that colorectal cancer in people in their early 20s or younger tends to be a more aggressive disease than that often seen in older people. "We do feel like it is a bit of a distinct disease than what we're seeing in older adults," said Dr. Erica Arnold , a pediatric surgery research fellow at Nationwide Children's Hospital in Columbus, Ohio. In October, Arnold presented new research on colorectal cancer in people ages 21 or younger at the annual meeting of the American Academy of Pediatrics . Arnold and her colleagues analyzed the cases of 84 patients diagnosed between 2012 and 2023. They found that the median age of diagnosis was 16 years old and the median duration of symptoms before diagnosis was only 12 weeks long. Only about 20% of the patients had a close relative with colorectal cancer, suggesting that for many of these young people, the disease did not necessarily emerge due to hereditary factors. If you want my honest opinion, it does suggest that these cancers are developing differently. Dr. Christopher Lieu, a professor of medical oncology at the University of Colorado Anschutz Eighty percent of the study participants were diagnosed with Stage III or Stage IV disease, meaning the cancer had already spread locally and to lymph nodes or to other, distant organs when the patients were diagnosed. For comparison, in colorectal cancer patients of all ages, 60% are diagnosed in Stage III or IV, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). In addition, Arnold said, one-third of the patients in their study had cellular markers of particularly aggressive cancer. "Some of that might be related to delays in diagnosis," Lieu said, "but if you want my honest opinion, it does suggest that these cancers are developing differently." The study's data was not nationally representative, but a recent analysis of CDC data has also found that colorectal cancer rates in youth are on the rise. In 1999, the diagnosis rate in kids ages 10 to 14 was 1 in a million. By 2020, it had risen to 6 in a million. For teens between 15 and 19, the rate of diagnosis went from 3 in a million to 13 in a million in that same time frame. Unclear causes There is no definitive reason for this rise, Lieu said. Research on the microbiome has suggested that processed food, antibiotic exposure in childhood , stress, reduced exercise and other lifestyle factors may contribute to this increased risk of colorectal cancer. Some microbes may play a particularly strong role, at least in some cases of colorectal cancer. For instance, a specific variant of the common gut bacterium Escherichia coli is strongly associated with colorectal cancer ; the variant carries a genetic segment and produces compounds that are toxic to genes. But this variant alone cannot explain all colorectal cancer cases in young people. Nor is it clear why the gut microbiome might be undergoing a shift in the first place. "It may be a combination of food, antibiotic use and environmental exposures," Lieu suggested. Regardless of the exact causes behind the cases, Arnold's new research pointed to the symptoms that deserve closer scrutiny in young people. Among the 84 patients in the study, 75% reported experiencing back and abdominal pain before their diagnosis, 45% had changes in their bowel movements, 43% experienced unexplained weight loss and 38% had rectal bleeding. Exclusive to Live Science Pro Rising temperatures could boost pregnancy risks worldwide — here's how Testosterone for menopause: The treatment is rising in popularity, but does it work? 'Mpox has not disappeared': Why the infectious disease is still spreading in the US and may be here to stay These are classic colorectal cancer symptoms, Arnold said, but they might be overlooked in this young age group because these same symptoms can have more common causes. Parents should know that in most cases, stomach pain and gastrointestinal disruptions in kids are not caused by colorectal cancer, Lieu said, calling the cancer an "extraordinarily rare event." Nevertheless, pain or gastrointestinal upset that doesn't ease or that worsens over time needs a checkup, and symptoms like weight loss and blood in the stool are very unusual in kids and deserve extra attention. "It's just important to investigate it to make sure we're catching colorectal cancer earlier rather than later in these patients," Arnold said. articles.title: NASA's Perseverance Rover Breaks the Distance Record for Driving Off-World
articles.summary: On October 11, NASA's Perseverance rover broke the record for the furthest distance traveled by a vehicle on another world. Initially set by NASA's Opportunity rover in 2014, Perseverance has now driven 28.1 miles, navigating—largely autonomously—boulder fields and sandpits on the Red Planet. We chatted with former Perseverance project scientist Ken Farley , the W. M. Keck Foundation Professor of Geochemistry at Caltech, about the rover's achievements and what the distance record means for Martian exploration. What has Perseverance been up to lately? We are at a very interesting place scientifically! The rock types where we are now are different than we've seen before, and they look very much like the kind of rock that one would expect the early Martian crust to have been made out of. These are likely extremely ancient rocks, older than rocks that we've looked at before—probably older than 4 billion years. There are few rocks on Earth older than 4 billion years. So we are in an area that is very deep in the history of the solar system. Perseverance has self-driving capabilities; what level of input do scientists give to the rover? First, scientists decide where we want the rover to go for scientific investigation by looking at detailed images of the Martian surface taken by orbiters in space. We can see where it's hilly, where it's rocky, where there are giant fields of sand, or cliffs. Engineers will then give the rover a rough sketch of a route to avoid big hazards, but the rover has to, by itself and based on imaging collected with the cameras and an algorithm, actually figure out how to go around rocks and minor obstacles. Though it is the most advanced technology that's off of Earth, it still has to take pictures and think about what it sees, where it's safe to go, where it's not safe to go, and how to drive around any hazards that it detects. articles.content: On October 11, NASA's Perseverance rover broke the record for the furthest distance traveled by a vehicle on another world. Initially set by NASA's Opportunity rover in 2014, Perseverance has now driven 28.1 miles, navigating—largely autonomously—boulder fields and sandpits on the Red Planet. We chatted with former Perseverance project scientist Ken Farley , the W. M. Keck Foundation Professor of Geochemistry at Caltech, about the rover's achievements and what the distance record means for Martian exploration. What has Perseverance been up to lately? We are at a very interesting place scientifically! The rock types where we are now are different than we've seen before, and they look very much like the kind of rock that one would expect the early Martian crust to have been made out of. These are likely extremely ancient rocks, older than rocks that we've looked at before—probably older than 4 billion years. There are few rocks on Earth older than 4 billion years. So we are in an area that is very deep in the history of the solar system. Perseverance has self-driving capabilities; what level of input do scientists give to the rover? First, scientists decide where we want the rover to go for scientific investigation by looking at detailed images of the Martian surface taken by orbiters in space. We can see where it's hilly, where it's rocky, where there are giant fields of sand, or cliffs. Engineers will then give the rover a rough sketch of a route to avoid big hazards, but the rover has to, by itself and based on imaging collected with the cameras and an algorithm, actually figure out how to go around rocks and minor obstacles. Though it is the most advanced technology that's off of Earth, it still has to take pictures and think about what it sees, where it's safe to go, where it's not safe to go, and how to drive around any hazards that it detects. It's a very slow process; the rover takes five or six hours to go about 100 meters as it's navigating its way through hazards. It's kind of like a self-driving car, except running on a very different and much slower computer. Perseverance is the size of an SUV, what kind of off-road capabilities does it have to handle the Martian surface? There's an interesting difference here between what it is possible to do and what it is best to avoid doing. If there's a rock that's bigger than, say, the size of a bowling ball, we go around it. If we have no choice, we can drive over it. The technical limit is much larger than that, but the goal, of course, is to keep the rover going for as long as possible by not overtaxing its capabilities. The absolute No. 1 rule for the rover is: Don't get yourself into a situation that you can't get out of. The rover has an enormous amount of onboard safety checks. One very common thing that happens is that the rover will drive up to an area where there's a whole bunch of bowling-ball-sized rocks that it is trying to drive across. In some cases, the rover will reach a limit—it will just say, "I don't know what the solution is. I can't get over the hazards that I'm sitting on or are in front of me, so I'm going to stop." A different kind of hazard is sand. As soon as the wheels start slipping significantly because of sand, the rover can tell, "My wheels are spinning, but I'm not going forward. I need to stop." The engineers on Earth can look at these situations and figure out how to get the rover out of it. At least on Perseverance, humans are always smarter than the rover. What kind of engineering enables a rover to achieve this kind of distance? One of the motivating scientific justifications for the mission has been to collect samples. If you're going to go to all the trouble to collect samples and then fly them to Earth, you want to get the biggest diversity you can, and that means covering a lot of ground. So, in the development stage of the mission, the rover was designed to be remarkably capable. Right from the get-go, the scientists decided that the mission should land inside Jezero Crater and explore the lake and river system there and then drive up the crater rim and drive around on the external part outside of the crater. Everyone's jaw dropped. People said, "Oh my god, it would be amazing to be able to do that, but no mission has ever driven that far." But the engineers put together an extremely capable vehicle. From a science point of view, it's been really, really successful. JPL has the capability to design things that are remarkably robust. The samples we've collected are really important, and I'm hoping that in the long run NASA will decide to retrieve them. A sample retrieval mission can teach us a lot about how to get to Mars and, importantly, to come back. If you want humans to be able to safely travel there, sample-return principles will be really useful. What's your perspective on sending humans to Mars? Will it happen in our lifetimes? Simply bringing back samples with a robotic mission is complicated, because you have to land something on Mars, then launch it back off and ferry it back to Earth. What are your hopes for the future of the Perseverance rover? The rover is currently in excellent health and testing has indicated that it is capable of continuing its mission lifespan. NASA's Curiosity rover has been going for 14 years, and we have every reason to believe that Perseverance will last at least as long as Curiosity. A major goal is collecting diverse samples. The more terrain and different geologic provinces you see, the more interesting things you can put in the sample collection, and the more interesting things that you can discover. My expectation is that we will continue to drive. Why is Mars important? There was water on the surface of Mars at the same time that life originated and expanded on Earth. If that happened on Earth, might it have happened on Mars? If not, why not? That's a really profound question. From a purely science perspective, Mars has a very long and rich geologic history in much the same way that Earth does, and we can use a lot of the tools that have been developed to understand Earth. People say that we need to study extrasolar planets for evidence of life, but the place that will give the richest information is the one you can bring samples from. Perseverance launched in the pandemic, in the summer of 2020. It was a heroic effort by JPL engineers to get Perseverance to the launchpad. We only have a launch period every two years, and if they hadn't gotten it to the launchpad, it would've cost hundreds of millions of dollars. You do not want to miss the launch period. When we successfully landed, the President made a statement about the importance to the American people of having done something great even in the pandemic. From my personal point of view, this is a purely human endeavor that is not profit-driven but driven by discovery. It allows us to go where we can never go individually, and everyone can feel good about it.

articles.title: Using light to control brain cells – neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth explains how he made his Nobel-winning discovery
articles.summary: Optogenetics, a field that started with an algae gene, is shedding light on new treatments for eye and neuropsychiatric conditions.
articles.content: Using light to control brain cells – neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth explains how he made his Nobel-winning discovery Skip to content Optogenetics involves the use of light to alter the activity of neurons. Westend61/Getty Images The 2026 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine honored Karl Deisseroth , Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their work developing optogenetics – a technique that allows researchers to control the activity of neurons with light. The Conversation Weekly podcast talked to Karl Deisseroth, a neuroscientist at Stanford University, about his journey developing optogenetics and its potential to treat a wide range of neuropsychiatric conditions. What follows is an edited transcript of the podcast. Take us back to the early 1990s. You’re training to be a doctor and you start a rotation working with psychiatric patients. What questions about the brain did that raise for you? Both basic neuroscience (people asking how the brain works) and clinical neuroscience (doctors trying to help people with brain disorders) have faced a very similar problem, which is the brain is quite mysterious and quite hard to study. It’s billions of fragile, transparent, very fast-acting cells, buried within the skull and doing very complex things. We don’t have a good model for how the brain works, unlike the heart, which is very obviously a pump . We don’t actually know what the brain’s trying to do. A lot of neuropsychiatric treatments are not as effective as they could be , and developing new ideas has been hard. The treatments we had were not grounded in a solid understanding of the cells involved. What are the cells actually doing? What are they trying to do? This was a problem that held back treatment. When I was in psychiatry training in the early 2000s, and also as a medical student in the late 1990s, I was very much impressed with the magnitude of the challenge. You went on to get a Ph.D. in neuroscience, and then you set up a lab at Stanford trying to understand how to control particular cells in the brain. What were the first experiments you did? I have a background in molecular biology, and I knew how to work with genes. So I was motivated to see if we could use genetics to make a treatment or an intervention that targets one kind of cell. Every cell has genes that tell it what to do. Different cells in the brain, just as other parts of the body, can be genetically targeted because different cells have different jobs. A cell that is a dopamine neuron has all the machinery needed to make the hormone dopamine. It uses different genes than a cell that makes the hormone serotonin, so they can be distinguished from each other. And so the thought was maybe I could have a way of controlling just the dopamine cells or just the serotonin cells by inserting a specific gene into them. But I didn’t know what would work well, so I tried inserting different types of genes into neurons. Inside this flask is the unicellular algae that played a critical role in the development of optogenetics. Tobias SchwarzSCHWARZ/AFP via Getty Images Some of the genes I tried were quite conventional; they were genes from mammals that I thought might affect the activity of neurons. But one was a gene from a single-celled algae – a microbe that converts light to energy. This gene coded for a light-activated protein called channelrhodopsin-2 that Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel identified a few years earlier. And I thought it was worth a try. It was the least likely to work, but why not try it? And amazingly, that was the one that worked. The genes that were lower risk didn’t work, and this gene from a single-cell microbe actually did. Walk us through what you did. You inserted the gene into rat cells, right? I had a preparation of cultured rodent neurons in a dish – basically a 24-well plate that let me look at many different conditions at the same time in different wells of this plate. This let me test side by side the conventional mammalian genes and this gene from the algae. So the first step was to get the genes into the cells. Then I exposed some plates of cells to light, while others I did not. I used a test to see which cells had activated. When I looked across the cells in the screen, I found that the ones that had the algae gene and had gotten light were showing this marker of activation, whereas the others had a much lower signal. That was a really thrilling moment because it showed that this gene from a photosynthetic single-celled organism – almost as far as you can possibly be from mammals evolutionarily – was working beautifully in fragile mammalian neurons. It was a moment of a lot of pressure and complexity, but also delight. Listen to Karl Deisseroth on The Conversation Weekly podcast . You went on to name your method optogenetics – the ability to control specific nerves using light in the brain – and you soon went on to using it to control living mice in various ways. What was it like in those first few years of working with live animals? The first experiment was in 2004 , but we didn’t show that it could control the behavior of freely moving mammals until 2007. So it took almost three years. But that first moment in 2007 was quite uplifting because that showed we had gone a big, big chunk of the way toward making it work. This was an experiment that was very visible and easy to understand. The right side of the brain controls the left side of the body and attention to the left side of the world. We put in a fiber optic into the right part of a mouse motor cortex – the part that controls movement – and when we flipped the switch, the mouse immediately began going left in circles. And then as soon as we turned off the laser light, it stopped and just looked up at us, as if nothing had happened. That, coupled with the first experiment – those were transcendent moments. What changed in your understanding of the brain in the moment you were able to switch particular neurons on and off? We understood that the technique would probably work to help us understand the brain better at that moment. And then we immediately started applying it to all sorts of different cells where things were mysterious – where nobody knew or couldn’t prove exactly what one cell type or another was doing in perception and cognition and action. We were able to find cells that were involved in hunger and thirst – basic survival drives. We were able to identify cells and pathways controlling aggression and defensiveness , parenting , how all the different parts of anxiety come on together and go away together, memory , motivation . The general applicability became clear over the subsequent years. Researchers are now using optogenetics in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment. How does that work? In 2010, two of my colleagues in Europe were interested in delivering one of these light-activated proteins to human eye samples – specifically the retina of the eye – which worked very well. So they did careful studies in monkeys and in people. And in 2021, just five years ago, they published a paper showing they could confer light sensitivity back to the retinas of a person who was completely blind from a neurodegenerative disease called retinitis pigmentosa . That’s what we call direct optogenetics . It’s somewhat complicated because you have to deliver the gene and light to the person. Karl Deisseroth, left, and his wife, Michelle Monje-Deisseroth, were at home when they were notified of his Nobel win. AP Photo/Noah Berger And going back to your psychiatric patients, who you still see in the clinic today, how do you hope optogenetics will be able to help them? There’s a much easier and more broadly impactful avenue that we call indirect optogenetics , which uses the knowledge that comes from studying which cells matter in a symptom and then designing medications that target those cells. This is something we’ve really lacked in neuropsychiatry for a long time. Indirect optogenetics is making strong headway for autism and schizophrenia . There are trials that are moving to their final stages for those disorders. My particular clinical specialty is autism, and I see the difficulties that come with irritability and anxiety in these patients. And I can see optogenetics leading to new medications that will help. articles.title: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email
articles.summary: For 3 days this month, 333 exit nodes were hacked in hopes of stealing sensitive data.
articles.content: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email - Ars Technica Skip to content Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday. The hijacking began in late August, when, according to Tor volunteers , the attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker then installed Ebury , a backdoor written for Linux that was discovered 12 years ago. Mysteries remain Then the attacker connected from the management server to a second Tor server, called Switzerland2, through SSH, using an RSA key that, for unknown reasons, investigators couldn’t find among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well. Finally, the attacker reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted. Ultimately, 333 exit relays were involved in the SSH and email interception campaign, although investigators haven’t established how the attackers gained control of all the underlying servers. The attackers then reconfigured the servers. One set of changes redirected SSH traffic traversing Tor to one of 12 attacker-controlled interceptor servers. Tor users who ignored warnings that the SSH host key had changed would then enter their SSH passwords. A second set of changes caused the exit nodes to block ports 25, 465, 587, 993, and 995—used to accept various forms of encrypted email—while continuing to allow ports for receiving unencrypted email. If email services downgraded the connections, the attackers used their access to the exit nodes to obtain unencrypted messages. It’s unclear whether any such downgrade attempts succeeded. The hijacking occurred from October 2 to October 5. Tor volunteers partially outlined the initial compromise of the management server and Switzerland2 and the attempt to intercept unencrypted email. Tuesday’s report revealed many new details, including how many exit nodes were compromised and how the attackers used them to redirect SSH traffic. “If you happen to get a circuit that exits over one of those 333 infected exit nodes, you won’t notice anything at first,” Kaba, the name of the Tor volunteer who authored the post, wrote. “Encrypted web traffic is forwarded as usual, but if you attempt an SSH connection over Port 22, you’re unknowingly redirected to one of 12 SSH interception servers. That’s exactly what happened to me on Friday morning.” Kaba then received the following warning: @@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@ @ WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED! @ @@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@ IT IS POSSIBLE THAT SOMEONE IS DOING SOMETHING NASTY! Someone could be eavesdropping on you right now (man-in-the-middle attack)! It is also possible that a host key has just been changed. The fingerprint for the ED25519 key sent by the remote host is SHA256:6baCZCPsl+AfQuujUS81fMEE/C7UeJ+AwjrImqmDB3E. Please contact your system administrator. The volunteer investigated further and found that when people ignored the warning, the attacker (1) stole the SSH password, (2) opened a connection to the server and observed all typed commands, and (3) opened a second connection and infected the server with Ebury. To investigate the campaign, Kaba created a script that polled all of Tor’s roughly 3,000 exit nodes to check whether they received a correct SSH fingerprint from a test server. The test server then checked whether the connection came from a pinned exit node or one of 12 SSH interception servers used by the attacker. The volunteer further set up a honeypot to observe the interception software attempting to log in and install Ebury. Several mysteries remain. Tor volunteers still don’t know how the attackers accessed so many servers. One possibility is that a company hosting them was hacked, but the theory is inconclusive. Another open question is who is behind the attack. “The use of Ebury and the broad collection of unencrypted data point to a financially motivated crime group,” Kaba wrote. “Though this too is just speculation.” A last perplexing finding: why did Switzerland2 accept an RSA key when there’s no evidence it was an authorized SSH certificate? The takeaway from the event is the crucial role in-depth defense plays in preventing data theft in mass hacks like this one. Those measures include configuring email accounts to accept only encrypted traffic and reject unencrypted ports. Another is to disable password authentication in favor of SSH keys. Dan Goodin Senior Security Editor Dan Goodin Senior Security Editor Dan Goodin is Senior Security Editor at Ars Technica, where he oversees coverage of malware, computer espionage, botnets, hardware hacking, encryption, and passwords. In his spare time, he enjoys gardening, cooking, and following the independent music scene. Dan is based in San Francisco. Follow him at here on Mastodon and here on Bluesky. Contact him on Signal at DanArs.82. 34 Comments Staff Picks Sorry for not having updated my knowledge of mail protocol for the last quarter-century. but isn't port 25 the one used for legacy SMTP (unencrypted mail)? You can initiate TLS encryption after connecting to a mail server in plain text on port 25 if it supports STARTTLS. https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc3207/#section-2 October 22, 2026 at 12:59 pm Comments Forum view Loading comments... articles.title: Spatially resolved tumor-microenvironment architecture defines therapeutic response in unresectable hepatoblastoma
articles.summary: Background: Hepatoblastoma exhibits variable therapeutic response that is not fully explained by current risk stratification. While prior studies have characterized tumor composition, the role of spatial organization in determining outcome, particularly in unresectable disease requiring transplantation under immunosuppression, remains unclear. Methods: We integrated spatial transcriptomics using the 10x Genomics Visium platform (n = 11 tumors) with single-cell spatial molecular imaging using NanoString CosMx (n = 3 tumors) on post-chemotherapy explant specimens across clinically defined groups (relapse-prone unresectable, non-relapse unresectable, and resectable hepatoblastoma). Spatial deconvolution, module scoring, spatial co-localization, and cell-cell interaction analyses were used to define region-level transcriptional programs and their underlying cellular organization. Results: We identified three spatial architectures associated with clinical outcome. Relapse-prone tumors exhibited a centralized, TME-dominated organization enriched for progenitor-like, cycling, and stress-responsive tumor cell states co-localized with SPP1+ TAMs and CAFs, with enrichment of hypoxia response, extracellular matrix remodeling, and Midkine (MDK-LRP1) signaling. Non-relapse tumors displayed a distributed architecture with compartmentalized tumor-immune interactions, increased immune engagement, and preserved epithelial differentiation, including inflammatory hepatocyte-like states. Resection samples showed reduced tumor cell state heterogeneity and more uniform TME-immune organization. Conclusions: Integration of regional and single-cell spatial transcriptomics across two platforms reveals that the chemo-remodeled tumor architecture of hepatoblastoma encodes spatially organized tumor cell-TME interactions as central determinants of therapeutic response.

enrichment.normalized_title: Spatially resolved tumor-microenvironment architecture defines therapeutic response in unresectable hepatoblastoma
enrichment.normalized_summary: Background: Hepatoblastoma exhibits variable therapeutic response that is not fully explained by current risk stratification. While prior studies have characterized tumor composition, the role of spatial organization in determining outcome, particularly in unresectable disease requiring transplantation under immunosuppression, remains unclear. Methods: We integrated spatial transcriptomics using the 10x Genomics Visium platform (n = 11 tumors) with single-cell spatial molecular imaging using NanoString CosMx (n = 3 tumors) on post-chemotherapy explant specimens across clinically defined groups (relapse-prone unresectable, non-relapse unresectable, and resectable hepatoblastoma). Spatial deconvolution, module scoring, spatial co-localization, and cell-cell interaction analyses were used to define region-level transcriptional programs and their underlying cellular organization. Results: We identified three spatial architectures associated with clinical outcome. Relapse-prone tumors exhibited a centralized, TME-dominated organization enriched for progenitor-like, cycling, and stress-responsive tumor cell states co-localized with SPP1+ TAMs and CAFs, with enrichment of hypoxia response, extracellular matrix remodeling, and Midkine (MDK-LRP1) signaling. Non-relapse tumors displayed a distributed architecture with compartmentalized tumor-immune interactions, increased immune engagement, and preserved epithelial differentiation, including inflammatory hepatocyte-like states. Resection samples showed reduced tumor cell state heterogeneity and more uniform TME-immune organization. Conclusions: Integration of regional and single-cell spatial transcriptomics across two platforms reveals that the chemo-remodeled tumor architecture of hepatoblastoma encodes spatially organized tumor cell-TME interactions as central determinants of therapeutic response.

articles.title: Pan-cancer remodeling of reactive oxygen species homeostasis: distinct roles of the ROS-generation and antioxidant arms in immune context and outcome
articles.summary: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are double-edged in cancer: tumor cells sustain high ROS generation while up-regulating antioxidant defense, so that the net balance between the two arms, rather than absolute ROS abundance, is the biologically meaningful quantity. Whether that balance defines a conserved tumor state across cancer types has been unclear. Here an experimentally measured ROS phenotype, obtained from a three-channel gold-nanocluster array, was generalized to public transcriptomes through a 107-gene ROS program scored in a large cell-line panel and in pan-cancer tumor and adjacent-normal tissue. The optical readout was reproducible and fully discriminative between cell lines, establishing the fingerprint as a quantitative starting point. In tumors, the generation and antioxidant arms were coordinately up-regulated relative to normal tissue, yet the two arms dissociated in their biology. The composite balance score tracked reduced immune infiltration consistently across cohorts, but arm-level decomposition showed that it was carried by low generation-arm activity in immune-cold tumors and followed arithmetically from how the balance score is defined; the association does not implicate antioxidant defense in immune infiltration. The clinical association pointed the other way: adverse outcome was attributable to the antioxidant arm, whereas generation was null. In cohort-held-out validation, tumors were separated from adjacent normal tissue, with redox programs outperforming generic phenotypic programs, indicating that the same program transfers across tumor types. Tumor remodeling of ROS homeostasis is therefore widespread, but its two arms carry distinct meanings: the balance score, driven by its generation term, reports immune context, whereas the antioxidant arm reports clinical risk.

articles.title: Productive, Durable, Fungible: How NVIDIA AI Factories Maximize Return on Investment
articles.summary: AI factories are built by the megawatt, even by the gigawatt. Each megawatt factory costs roughly $60 million, and AI factory operators will only commit capital on that scale with a clear view of the return on investment. Three key things shape AI factory returns: Earning capacity: What the factory could earn in a year [...]
articles.content: Productive, Durable, Fungible: How NVIDIA AI Factories Maximize Return on Investment | NVIDIA Blog Skip to content AI factories are built by the megawatt, even by the gigawatt. Each megawatt factory costs roughly $60 million, and AI factory operators will only commit capital on that scale with a clear view of the return on investment. Three key things shape AI factory returns: Earning capacity: What the factory could earn in a year if it sold every token it can produce. Useful life : How long its AI hardware keeps earning. Demand : How much demand there is for those tokens. Strength cannot fully offset weakness in another. High earning capacity counts for little if the factory sells only part of what it can produce. High demand matters little if it stops producing at full capacity in just a year. Nor are the three independent. A factory that can run more kinds of workloads finds more demand, keeping it earning year after year. NVIDIA AI factories are engineered to maximize all three. They’re: Productive : Delivering the highest throughput per megawatt and the lowest cost per token, which maximizes their earning capacity . Durable : NVIDIA GPUs and systems keep earning years after they ship, extending useful life . Fungible : They run every type of AI — in every phase and every place — as well as many workloads that don’t involve AI at all, which deepens and broadens the demand they can serve. NVIDIA platform is productive, durable and fungible, which maximizes AI factory returns. Engineering codesign across the full stack maximizes AI factory throughput, and continuous software optimization keeps installed hardware productive years after it ships. NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries let a factory run any accelerated workload. A standardized architecture then puts all of it within reach of any operator, deployable from a validated reference design. Productive: Highest Tokens Per Megawatt and Lowest Token Cost Power is the binding constraint on an AI factory. This makes tokens per second per megawatt the number that governs earning capacity. More tokens inside a fixed power envelope means more revenue. Lower cost per token means more margin on it. SemiAnalysis AgentX data shows NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems deliver over 30x higher throughput per megawatt than NVIDIA GB300 NVL72, and up to 45x lower cost per million tokens on the DeepSeek V4 Pro model. Gains of that size come from extreme codesign across the full stack: from models and workloads down through software to compute, networking and memory, all optimized together. SemiAnalysis AgentX analysis about NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 performance for GLM 5.3. Two questions follow. If every generation makes tokens dramatically cheaper, does demand for compute shrink? No, it expands. Cheaper tokens make more use cases economical, and those use cases consume more tokens than the efficiency saved. The second question is about durability. If each generation is so much better than the last, what happens to the older generations? Durable: The Installed Base Keeps Earning Not every workload needs the newest system. The right fit depends on a workload’s complexity and shape, which is why the last generation keeps earning after the next one arrives. The NVIDIA A100 GPU shipped in 2020 and is still in commercial service six years later, demonstrating its continued economic value; CoreWeave recently extended bookings for units first introduced in 2020 through 2029. Over the years, every major operator has extended the depreciation schedule on its servers, which is a guess about when hardware stops earning, and one that keeps moving out. A September 2026 Sprout analysis, “ The Productive Life of a Data Center GPU ,” tracks how that schedule has shifted across every major operator. Every major operator has extended server life. Source: Sprout, “The Productive Life of a Data Center GPU,” September 2026. Data based on company disclosures and press reporting compiled by Sprout. Accounting life is a conservative proxy for physical life — Microsoft’s NVIDIA V100 fleet ran 8.4 years against a six-year book life. Barkr puts useful life at five to six years for an eight-GPU H100 system and nine to 10 years for GB300 NVL72, based on what those systems resell for. Silicon Data shows a six-year-old A100 GPU is still worth a quarter of what it cost, where a five-year depreciation schedule had it at zero more than a year ago. Ornn Data finds the market paying 80% as much to rent an A100 GPU on a five-year contract as on a one-month contract. CUDA , the software platform with which NVIDIA GPUs are programmed, runs across generations, so nothing an operator already owns is stranded when a new architecture arrives. Continuous software and kernel optimization keeps improving what existing hardware can do. The same platform runs machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, reasoning, agentic AI and physical AI. Each new kind of work arrived on hardware that was already installed. That’s fungibility. The more kinds of work a system can take, the longer it keeps finding work. Fungible: Every Type of AI, Every Phase, Every Place A factory built for one kind of work is a bet that the work stays. A factory that runs everything stays useful and revenue-generating even when the work changes. NVIDIA AI factories run every type of AI model — open and proprietary — across language, vision, biology, physics and robotics. They run every phase, from data processing through pretraining, post-training and inference. And they run in every place, from hyperscale and AI clouds to sovereign programs, enterprise data centers and the edge. The NVIDIA platform is fungible and runs every type of AI workload, in every phase and place. Not all of it is building and running AI models. The same infrastructure runs data processing, scientific computing, simulation, graphics and more. All of those workloads, AI and non-AI alike, reduce to the same parallel math, and NVIDIA GPUs are built to run exactly that across thousands of cores at once. CUDA is why one chip can simulate light, fold a protein and predict the next token. More than 1,000 ready-made CUDA-X libraries and models sit on top, covering everything from deep neural networks, computational lithography and quantum circuit simulation to vector search and climate modeling, with more than 10 million developers building on them. That’s what makes NVIDIA GPUs general-purpose accelerated computing rather than a custom ASIC built for one workload. Being general purpose does not mean being generic: Tensor Cores and the Transformer Engine put AI-optimized hardware inside a programmable architecture, delivering specialization and flexibility in one chip. One architecture running all of it is what keeps utilization high, and the return with it. This versatility shows up in production across customers: Lilly : Building and running protein, small-molecule and genomics models on a 1,016-GPU, on-premises cluster, plus chatbots and agentic workflows for its own teams. Pinterest : Post-training and deploying a vision language model on a hyperscale cloud, across 14,000 GPUs spanning NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper and earlier architectures. Revolut : Processing data for billions of transaction records with NVIDIA cuDF, then training and deploying a foundation model on an AI cloud. Runway : Training a world model on NVIDIA Hopper and serving on the NVIDIA Blackwell platform using cloud infrastructure. Texas A&M University : Running molecular simulation and AI drug discovery on its supercomputer, at 95-98% utilization across 26 projects and seven institutions. The same is true beyond AI. Cosm operates a distributed NVIDIA-powered data center providing flexible compute resources across high-resolution video playback, streaming, real-time graphics and synchronized display. Dassault Systèmes powers the virtual twin simulation behind aircraft certification at Wichita State and vehicle design at Lucid Motors. And Unilever builds product imagery from digital twins rather than photo shoots, cutting production costs in half. No list of examples here would be complete — that’s the point. NVIDIA AI factories are engineered to be productive, durable and fungible: more profitable tokens, longer useful life and deeper demand. That’s what maximizes their return. Learn more about NVIDIA AI factories by tuning in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST. articles.summary: Microsoft is announcing its third-generation Maia in-house AI chip today, designed to be the "primary AI inference system" for Microsoft's products and services. articles.content: Microsoft’s new AI chip makes it less reliant on Nvidia’s GPUs | The Verge Skip to main content The homepage The homepage Navigation Drawer Login / Sign Up close Search Light System Dark Subscribe Comments Drawer Comments Loading comments Getting the conversation ready... News AI Gadgets Microsoft’s new AI chip makes it less reliant on Nvidia’s GPUs The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027. The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027. by Tom Warren Oct 12, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Microsoft’s Maia 300 chip. Image: Microsoft Tom Warren is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad , who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years. Microsoft is announcing its third-generation Maia in-house AI chip today, designed to be the “primary AI inference system” for Microsoft’s products and services. Maia 300 not only improves the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud, it’s also more capable of handling the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks. Maia 300 will start being rolled out to production in 2027, and it has been designed with efficiency in mind. “We expect Maia 300 to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems,” says Scott Guthrie , executive vice president of Microsoft’s cloud group. “And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.” These efficiency improvements will allow Microsoft to rely mainly on its in-house AI chips soon, instead of ones from Nvidia and AMD. “We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services,” says Guthrie. Maia 300 chips will start being used for production workloads in 2027. Image: Microsoft Maia 300 is a successor to the 200, which was only announced in January . Maia 200 is already running on production AI workloads across Microsoft, including Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and Microsoft’s own AI models. “Maia 200 is the best performing AI infrastructure in our fleet, measured in real world metrics for AI services,” says Guthrie. “Maia 300 is a complete AI system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks.” Related Microsoft is finally making custom chips — and they’re all about AI Microsoft’s latest AI chip goes head-to-head with Amazon and Google Microsoft is using a new chiplet architecture to get its all-important efficiency gains. Built on TSMC’s N2P process node, the latest Maia 300 architecture separates compute, memory controller, and I/O functions. “This increases the silicon area dedicated to compute performance and allows each function to use the technology best suited to its role,” says the Azure hardware and infrastructure team. Maia 300 is also a key part of Microsoft’s own AI model work, and could help the company achieve its goal of catching up with Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic. “We have to work across the full stack, all the way down to the silicon,” says Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. “At that scale we need a platform that we own, and that we co-design with our models. That’s why running our Microsoft AI models on top of the Maia chip is a critical focus for our team.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. articles.title: Possible Vulnerability in Apple’s Automatic Reboot
articles.summary: 404Media is reporting (alternate link ) that a cyber-weapons arms manufacturer is exploiting a vulnerability in iOS to bypass its automatic reboot security feature. This is the feature that automatically puts an iPhone into a more secure state if it hasn’t been used for 72 hours. The new technology to get around inactivity reboot was developed by Magnet Forensics, the company behind GrayKey, a popular tool sold to law enforcement agencies that allows them to unlock and access data stored in iPhones and Android smartphones . Magnet has developed a new device called GrayKey Preserve and a feature for its regular GrayKey devices called Evidence Preservation Mode, according to the video...
articles.content: Possible Vulnerability in Apple's Automatic Reboot - Schneier on Security Home Blog Possible Vulnerability in Apple’s Automatic Reboot 404Media is reporting (alternate link ) that a cyber-weapons arms manufacturer is exploiting a vulnerability in iOS to bypass its automatic reboot security feature. This is the feature that automatically puts an iPhone into a more secure state if it hasn’t been used for 72 hours. The new technology to get around inactivity reboot was developed by Magnet Forensics, the company behind GrayKey, a popular tool sold to law enforcement agencies that allows them to unlock and access data stored in iPhones and Android smartphones . Magnet has developed a new device called GrayKey Preserve and a feature for its regular GrayKey devices called Evidence Preservation Mode, according to the video. “This is an absolute game changer for iOS forensics and a function that I wish we had years ago,” a Magnet employee says in the leaked video, specifically mentioning that the solution is targeted at the iPhone’s inactivity reboot feature and the data it makes unavailable. GrayKey Preserve and Evidence Preservation Mode are also designed to combat another iPhone feature that automatically deletes certain data ­- such as cached locations, and recently deleted photos and iMessages ­- after a certain number of days. “We’re gonna be able to preserve that data for an infinite amount of time.” Presumably, now that Apple engineers know that this flaw exists they can find and fix it. AI turns out to be really good at this sort of thing. Another news article . Tags: iPhone , law enforcement , police , vulnerabilities Posted on October 6, 2026 at 7:06 AM • 14 Comments Comments Celos • October 6, 2026 9:51 AM Just the usual reminder: Do NOT trust your phone. The attackers and their supporters cannot stand you keeping any secrets and hence they will do whatever they can to break in. Bob • October 6, 2026 9:57 AM Bet it’s a Faraday cage with a cell site simulator whose clock doesn’t progress. KC • October 6, 2026 10:56 AM Interesting. Here are some supposed natural expiration timelines of certain iOS data. Eg, cached locations 7 days, recently deleted iMessages 30 days, etc. lurker • October 6, 2026 1:36 PM “… another iPhone feature that automatically deletes certain data ­- … and recently deleted photos and iMessages ­- after a certain number of days.” Whatever happened to rm ? Yeah, I know, it’s in the “Trash” can. Clive Robinson • October 6, 2026 4:08 PM @ ALL, On the assumption the clock is involved, one way to do this is to “stop the clock” or keep resetting the clock time back just a couple of minutes or longer. Another way is a bit more subtle, any CRUD access to memory generally means at least a two step process of the application writing to a buffer and the OS then writing the buffer to the memory. The reason for this is to keep the memory in a sane state. An OS generally uses some form of signals mediated “Inter Process Communication”. Thus has flags tucked away in the OS to control the signals to App Buffer Memory. If you block those signals by blocking the flags or flag mechanism then the memory does not get updated by a “Create, Update, or Delete” action. The way to get around the issue is quite old and was used in Mil Kit back in the 1980s and I assume later. You actually do this by encrypting the data contents of every memory object with it’s own key. If you delete or change the key at any time it mostly does not do any harm even to open Apps as long as the most basic of meta-data is not damaged… It must be a decade and a half or more since we discussed the issues with memory encryption on this blog, as it’s something that has in effect been abstracted away in more modern OS’s and Systems. The last time I remember was with “a snake eating it’s tail”(Ouroboros). The idea being that you actually re-encrypted blocks of memory by having the keys cycle around. With part of the key held in memory and the other part held via a CPU register, as a way to get around the LNO attack on DRAM and SRAM that had had power removed. cybershow • October 6, 2026 8:44 PM @Bob That half makes sense, but why would the device listen to network time instead of its own internal clock? Network time suddenly standing still would count as suspicious and trigger a wipe, no? The only hope of freezing the internal time is to drop it into liquid helium. lurker • October 6, 2026 10:41 PM @cybershow “why would the device listen to network time instead of its own internal clock?” Sometimes so-called developers do the darndest things. I’ve seen a FM radio receiver in a de-Googled “privacy” phone that goes out looking for ntp time. Local wall clock ain’t good enough … freedom • October 6, 2026 11:13 PM The assumption here seems to be that crapple “products” (i.e. malware) can be “trusted”, which is of course a ridiculous assumption. I wonder why there is no actual discussion about actually solving the problems caused by the NSA-GCHQ-corporate mafia. Fake French Spy • October 6, 2026 11:25 PM @lurker • October 6, 2026 10:41 PM what you and some other geniuses round here don’t mention is that the CMOS battery gets weaker over time making the system clock more and more inaccurate so to help out with that our computer “forefathers” came up with the concept behind port 123 to SYNC the local time with one of the time servers automagically unless you own an older system and have the luxury of disabling that service or blocking port 123 in yr FW. lurker • October 7, 2026 1:40 AM @Fake French Spy Yebbut, the operating system is supposed/allowed to do that, and then provide a sufficiently reliable system clock so that random apps and service don’t create security risks by wandering over the net unattended. Hacketry • October 7, 2026 2:40 AM That kind of thing is kind of old, any software can be hacked, directly or what it does in the computer, meaning hack the computer. Example: software with a ‘FREE 30-day trial’ or the computer it resides in (or both) can be hacked to extend that ’30-day trial’ to many years. That is not just conjecture, it has been done. Clive Robinson • October 7, 2026 10:27 AM @ Hacketry, ALL, With regards, “… any software can be hacked, directly or what it does in the computer…” Actually depending on what you mean by “software” and “computer” that might not be true. Those old enough to have worked in FMCE as design engineers back into the mid 1990’s and earlier will have used “Mask Programmable Microcontrollers”. Those working on lower production runs would have used the equivalent of a diode “fuse programmable array. Untill much the same time the BIOS and similar for Personal Computers were written into either ROM or EPROM. But on boot up the code in them would copy down into RAM which then made them vulnerable in the way you are suggesting. Even today comparatively hard as they are to get now, there are still actual ROM or PROM parts you can get in Mil Spec byte-wide parts that are not Flash or “Electrically Erasable PROM”(EEPROM). I use them in CubSat and other HiRel and HiSec designs where code should not be alterable. The other issue is “control Flags” for signals and buffers as I mentioned above, they are also usually RAM based and thus vulnerable. Moving them to X Thus the trick is to design systems where executable code can not run in RAM and where control instructions (think branches in ASM) can not be available from RAM. This way malware has nowhere to go in the system, and software can not be changed by it. Basically you have to think of the memory in a secure system as ranging from “fully mutable” to being “immutable”. You want executable code in “immutable memory”. Likewise control flags and similar to being where possible in CPU registers only. One more modern trick you see in some systems where security is considered important but code needs to be changed is to have an encryption key chain system where the executable code is encrypted in a way that if it gets changed it fails to decrypt and execute. freedom • October 7, 2026 11:59 AM CMOS battery gets weaker over time making the system clock more and more inaccurate That is patently false. The clock is controlled by a quartz crystal. Clive Robinson • October 7, 2026 10:52 PM @ cybershow, Bob, ALL, With regards, “The only hope of freezing the internal time is to drop it into liquid helium.” Actually not quite true… Apple has used and I assume still uses “MEMS” devices that are supposedly hermetically sealed and physically smaller than even the smallest of 32Khz quartz “clock crystals” and other sensors such as gyros that use “mechanical strain or resonance” for basic operation. Only “hermetically sealed” even “vacuum sealed” does not mean sealed against certain very small atoms such as hydrogen[1] and helium used as cryo-coolants and party balloons that people have been known to use to make their voice sound like a cartoon chipmunk / Donald Duck… There is a reported case from 2018 of a US hospital dumping it’s MRI machine cryo-coolant inadvertantly into the hospital internal air rather than to directly outside the building. Then people with Apple phones and other devices experiencing very odd behaviour, https://www.ifixit.com/News/11986/iphones-are-allergic-to-helium What is not reported is how staff and patients felt. Both Helium and Hydrogen displace oxygen in your respiratory system and whilst helium gas won’t poison you, they both will effectively drown you (Inert gas asphyxiation)… But another thing to note. Apple OS’s used in these devices is not a traditional style multi-tasking OS. I’m not going to go into details you can look it up. But it did enable Apple to pull a dirty trick back in 2017 on it’s users called “BatteryGate” at the time, for which it finally got fined by the French in 2020. https://www.ifixit.com/News/35519/apple-has-been-fined-e25-million-for-deliberately-slowing-down-iphones-in-2017 [1] Hydrogen is a pesky gas and even worse atom. It only has a single electron that can be fairly easily stripped away when it “ionises” chemically or electrically to “atomic hydrogen” leaving just the nucleus which is a proton. When it gets the electron back it reverts to “molecular hydrogen” and it’s very much larger size… Thus can create fairly serious mechanical stress and structural breakdown of materials at the molecular level in steel etc. The process is known as “hydrogen embrittlement”, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_embrittlement And it’s the curse of both industrial chemical and nuclear engineers who have to design plant installations, https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/1185588 Hydrogen gas in the normal environment atmosphere is also something electrical/electronics engineers have to keep in mind when designing “Intrinsically Safe”(IS or ‘Ex i’) or “flame proof”(Ex d) equipment as a mixture of hydrogen and other gases such as oxygen can make quite a pop even with very small electrical charges, as I know from personal experience with “IS certification testing” “blowing the bell jar”. enrichment.normalized_title: Possible Vulnerability in Apple’s Automatic Reboot
enrichment.normalized_summary: 404Media is reporting (alternate link ) that a cyber-weapons arms manufacturer is exploiting a vulnerability in iOS to bypass its automatic reboot security feature. This is the feature that automatically puts an iPhone into a more secure state if it hasn’t been used for 72 hours. The new technology to get around inactivity reboot was developed by Magnet Forensics, the company behind GrayKey, a popular tool sold to law enforcement agencies that allows them to unlock and access data stored in iPhones and Android smartphones . Magnet has developed a new device called GrayKey Preserve and a feature for its regular GrayKey devices called Evidence Preservation Mode, according to the video...

articles.title: I Tested Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra. The Local AI Performance Is Remarkable.
articles.summary: Powered by NVIDIA's RTX Spark N1X, Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra can do something that still feels a little absurd: run huge local AI models on a laptop without making everyday work miserable. After extensive testing, I'm impressed.
articles.content: I Tested Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra.
